In English, it says employment equity.
Mr. Speaker, I have another example in Section 4 of the same Bill, where we read in English:

"Plant employment equity by ..."

But in French, it reads:
L'employeur vise a i'equite professionnelle par les actions suivantes:
Mr. Speaker, "vise" implies an objective but not an obligation.
Mr. Speaker, this is a distortion. There is a distinct difference between the two versions. Mr. Speaker, there is a lot of discrimination against women here in Canada. In the Abella Report, in Table 5, we read that in the executive and administrative groups only 25 per cent are Canadian women, while 75 per cent are men; in the technical, scientific and mathematic groups, only 14 per cent are Canadian women. In Table 10, the Report says that the gap between men's and women's salaries is enormous, when we consider that the average income of women is only 64 per cent of that for men here in Canada. In her report, Judge Abella also says there are many similar statistics that demonstrate very clearly that discrimination exists against native peoples, visible minorities and the handicapped in this country.
The Canadian experience in affirmative action programs is very short compared to that in the United States. In the United States they had voluntary affirmative action programs for many years. About 25 years ago they decided that they had to have mandatory programs which were enforced because voluntary programs were not working at all.
I have an article which was in The Globe and Mail very recently. The headline is, "U.S. Big Business Bullish on Affirmative Action Laws". In the United States they found that if
October 3, 1985

affirmative action programs are mandatory it is good for big business, for the economy, and for making a profit. Despite the fact that Ronald Reagan has recently been trying to backtrack on some of the mandatory aspects of affirmative action laws in the United States, big business sees it as a very good thing.
In this country we have tried voluntary equal employment opportunity programs in the past. In most cases they have not been very effective. Judge Abella relates in her report how the proportion of women or minority groups which she studied has not been increased in terms of job opportunities and that discrimination has not really lessened in our country despite voluntary programs. We have the Human Rights Commission and human rights laws, but they only act when someone files a complaint. That is why we need some mandatory action in this country.
I think that Bill C-62 is a signpost that the Government has not really learned that voluntary affirmative action programs do not work. It has not really learned from the American experience and it has not really understood what Judge Abella is saying in her report. Mr. Speaker, the Government is trying to reinvent the wheel. It is trying to do the same old thing that has not worked in this country for years and years. This Bill is only a timid step forward which will not change things in any substantive way. The only part of the program that is mandatory is the reporting procedure and there is a $50,000 fine if someone does not report what they are doing in terms of affirmative action. That is all there is in the Bill and both of the Ministers responsible are fully aware of that.
The working paper of the Minister herself which was issued some time ago says that employers will not have to submit specific operational plans for approval by Government or report on specific initiatives. The Minister is saying that there is only the court of pulic opinion. She says that if it is publicized that Company A is doing a bad thing by not hiring enough women or Canadians from various minority groups, the sheer force of public opinion will force it to change its mind. That has not worked in the past, it has not worked in the United States, and I suggest that it is not going to work here now because there are no penalties. It will not bring fairness or more jobs to this country. In fact, on page 195 of her report, Judge Abella said that voluntary programs do not work. The Minister often speaks of this excellent report of Judge Abella and I will quote from it. It reads:
A voluntary program with a mandatory reporting requirements is nonetheless voluntary in the absence of a requirement to remedy the discriminatory practices disclosed by the information reported.
She says that it is still a voluntary program if reporting is all that is required. In her report she says time and again that it must be mandatory, that there must be timetables, and that we must ensure that the employment equity requirements are enforced by law. That is why we need mandatory affirmative action in this country.
Another thing we need is an enforcement agency, which we do not now have. We have no goals or timetables. All of this is so despite the fact that the Prime Minister, when he was
Employment Equity
campaigning as Leader of the Opposition, promised that we would have goals, timetables, and objectives in this country to bring about greater fairness for the women of Canada. He said:
We support the need for effective human resource planning within the federal bureaucracy which includes goals and objectives to achieve parity for women at all levels of government operations commensurate with their skills and expectations. Numerical goals are one of the several measures required. Training and retraining are others.
Where are the numerical goals, where are the targets, where is the timetable, where is the fulfillment of this particular election campaign? I do not see it, Mr. Speaker. It is another promise made and another promise broken by the Prime Minister of Canada. Time and again reference was made to the need for goals and objecties by Judge Abella, the Americans, women, other groups in our society, and the Prime Minister in his appeal for votes. Yet, it is not in the legislation introduced by the Government.
We have heard much talk about the Prime Minister being a union man, representing working people, and driving a truck on the north shore of the St. Lawrence. We hear that he believes in participatory democracy and that people should have more involvement in their own lives. Yet there is no mention whatsoever of the fact that workers who are unionized can have any participation whatsoever in achieving the goals of employment equity. Why is it that, through their unions in a co-operative way, workers cannot participate in achieving the goals of employment equity on behalf of women or other groups which are mentioned in this particular Bill?
I would also like to discuss contract compliance. Last March and April the Minister made much of the need for contract compliance, of the fact that the Government spends billions of dollars a year buying goods and services, and of the fact that we need more awareness of affirmative action programs by the companies from which we purchase goods and services. Yet, there is nothing to force companies to comply with what the Government wants them to comply with. There is nothing mandatory. There is no penalty. In the United States there is mandatory contract compliance. As I said before, in Canada it is voluntary for companies with over 100 employees or contracts of over $200,000. Why not make it mandatory? Does the Government not believe that that should be the case?
I went back through my records and I see another promise made by the Prime Minister when he was Leader of the Opposition. That guy made a lot of promises, some 300-odd.
Three hundred and thirty-eight.

Three hundred and thirty-eight promises. When appealing for the votes of women last summer he said the following with regard to contract compliance:
When seeking government business, these companies will be required to detail their action plans, timetables and programs for attracting, training and advancing women within their operations. This, in my view, is a legitimate and fair requirement.
I ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) to show us any clause in the Bill which will put into law the promise of the Prime Minister that these compa-

October 3, 1985
Employment Equity
nies will be required to detail their action plans rather than merely to report on what they have done for affirmative action employment equity. I see that one Conservative Member of Parliament is so embarrassed he is already over here on the opposition benches. The Prime Minister said that they would be required to detail their action plans, timetables, and programs for attracting, training and advancing women. If you get elected because you have made certain promises and commitments to the people, then I think you should keep those promises in the legislation you bring forward. It is no wonder that the people are becoming very cynical about this Prime Minister. Did he hear about the tuna? Did he hear about a Minister resigning? What did he say about old age pensions? What is he saying about family allowances? I know that the Minister herself would not break a campaign promise, but she is afraid to take a tough stand against the Prime Minister, or she has tried and cannot do it.
Are you kidding?

One of the back-benchers says: Are you kidding? That is a pretty big insult against the Minister. I have more confidence in her than he does. I am sure she has fought for this promise. I am sure she stood up in Cabinet and tried to point out to the Prime Minister that he made a promise of goals and objectives and timetables.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: And he is delivering. Where was the NDP? It was silent.

The NDP has not been silent. We have said many times in this House and in the campaign that you must have mandatory goals and targets and objectives. The Prime Minister said, "That is a good idea, Ed". He made that promise and commitment himself. So once again I ask the people of Canada to contact the Conservative Members of Parliament and the Minister and tell them to keep their word. It is a sacred trust, the Prime Minister said. Well, keep your promise to the women and other people of this country. When we talk about affirmative action in contract compliance we are talking about some $12 billion a year of government expenditures, if not more. That is a lot of money, a lot of influence and a lot of impact this Government can have on the private sector from coast to coast.
I said before that I do not think the Bill is comprehensive enough. The whole concept of equal pay for work of equal value is not being enforced in this country as it should be. I do not think you can have any kind of employment equity without a comprehensive Bill which makes sure we have equal pay for work of equal value. We also need more money for daycare. The Minister herself knows that more and more mothers are working when they have small children. Judge Abella said in her report that in 1980 there were some 760,000 children under the age of six whose mothers are in the workforce. We do not have adequate daycare centres in this country.
I think there should also be more initiatives at the federal level to co-operate with the provinces on employment equity and getting rid of discrimination.
Where was the NDP Government in Manitoba?

In that way we can have greater social equity in this country, if I can coin a phrase. We still have tremendous discrimination in access to education for people from poorer families, native families, and all kinds of other groups. We do not have equal access to training in this country. We have all kinds of discrimination against disabled Canadians. You can see this in the architectural design of our buildings and the fact that there are all kinds of public services not available to them. We have all kinds of additional costs for disabled Canadians. We should be taking a lot more action and stronger stands on matters of social equity.
I am very disappointed that the Minister is not implementing the recommendations of Judge Abella to make sure that we have mandatory employment equity in Canada. As I said before, we can quote page after page where she says we need it, that voluntary employment equity and affirmative action will not work. As the Prime Minister said in the campaign, we need to have it in force and written into the law. I ask her why she is so timid. Why is she taking this very tiny step when she has a massive majority and a mandate to act and when she has an absolutely excellent report by Judge Abella to use as an authority? We need timetables, goals and objectives, and we need enforcement. You cannot just go to a big company like General Motors or any other company-perhaps the tuna affair is a good example-and say that we are expecting it to implement affirmative action.
These programs are becoming more and more important as time goes on. We have a changing world economy, world-wide recessions, along with the whole problem of international finances. When unemployment is created it is usually the disadvantaged groups who are laid off first. That is another reason why we need some mandatory affirmative action. Then we have technological change, jobs which are disappearing very rapidly. We have automation in the offices and in banks. Once again it is women and disadvantaged minority groups who are the first to be laid off. We do not want to create more and more job ghettoes in Canada, and it is for those reasons that we must have goals and enforcement if we are to achieve fairness in this country and create more jobs for one and all.
I want to conclude by saying that I have always believed that if you give people the tools and treat them equally, they will build a tremendous country for one and all. They will make a contribution to our society which will make us all proud. Certainly it is the role of the Government to enforce equality and fairness.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me this morning to have an opportunity to speak on this very important Bill, and I hope to deal with some of the misconceptions which have been portrayed by Members on the
October 3, 1985

opposite side of the House about the objectives of this Bill. As we know, at this point we are talking about the principles of the Bill and I think I can speak with some authority. For a number of years I was actually involved in the development and implementation of employment equity programs, both for women and for native people. I know what it is like on the ground to have to do it, not just to mouth the words of criticism we hear in this place. It is a lot more difficult than perhaps the Hon. Member on the other side of the House would have us believe.
During the past six months I have been fortunate as a member of the Special Committee on Equality Rights to travel across the country and hear representatives of the target groups included in this Bill. I have heard from women's groups, visible minority groups, the handicapped and native people. I heard their concerns about achieving equality of opportunity and employment equity and I would like to address some of those concerns as well. In addition, we heard from other Canadians who had great fears and misunderstandings about employment equity, and we have a responsibility as parliamentarians to address those fears and concerns as well. From what I have heard in the House so far this morning, I think there is as much misunderstanding in this House as there is among the general public about what employment equity is all about and the best way of achieving it. I will come back to these points later, but I want to assure my hon. colleagues that the Bill before us does provide for mandatory employment equity and an enforcement mechanism.
There has been lots of talk for many years about employment equity. I know that 25 years ago when I entered the workforce it certainly was not easy. We were saying that there should be more opportunities for women. But how do you go about doing that in effective ways? My colleagues on the opposite side had, of course, many years in which to address this subject and there were a number of reports which brought to their attention the inequities and problems, but really very little was done. It is only in the last year that positive action has been taken on the part of this Government to show our commitment to all Canadians to provide for employment equity.
The report of Judge Abella has been discussed in the House this morning. It was an excellent report by an outstanding woman of our society. It was laid before the House in November, and the Minister of Employment and Immigration provided a comprehensive response in March outlining the focus of Government initiatives. In June of this year we tabled the legislation and we are now debating it. I hope that we will see early passage and we do not waste more opportunities for more groups, many of whom have appeared before various government committees in the past. I would like to see us get on with this very quickly.
I would like to address the points I heard from across the country, and there are points of concern that come from my constituency, about why we need this legislation. Perhaps for
Employment Equity
most of us here it is easy to understand that, but there are some Canadians who do not understand. They see Canadian society as a society which prizes individual freedom and individual responsibility. They ask, why are special actions needed for certain Canadians? We had the myth that if you had a strong back, common sense and determination, you could do anything you wanted to do. The Horatio Alger myth is perpetrated in Canada and a lot of people think that that is the way you should do it, a lot of women, too.
We had women appearing before our equality rights committee who said "I don't want special treatment. I got there on my own. I don't think the Government needs to do anything for us". We have a responsibility to listen to those people as well. Unfortunately, the facts that we know are different.
As Sherry Stein of the Coalition for Employment Equity for Disabled Persons who expressed her view before our committee said:
In an ideal society you do not need affirmative action. But in a society such as ours, where it has been recognized that certain groups of people, including handicapped adults, are at a disadvantage, you do need some kind of measure to catch up to bring these people to a point of equal competition on the job market.
We know also from statistics that there are many groups of disadvantaged. We know that 77 per cent of women in the labour force are in only five of the 22 major job categories. In 1982, a woman with a university degree earned the same as a man with a high school education. Whites have three job prospects for every one for blacks.
My colleague earlier this morning referred to a report done in metropolitan Toronto about discrimination on the basis of race. We know that, unfortunately, it exists in our society still. We know that among employable disabled persons, 50 per cent are unemployed. We know that in many native communities, unemployment is higher than 70 per cent.
Clearly action is required. Also, action, as the Minister said earlier, makes economic sense. We feel all Canadians have a stake in our economic society, that they should have the opportunity to participate and to add to the wealth of society.
It is also consistent with the very beliefs outlined in Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms that we should have positive action to ensure that all Canadians have equal opportunity. We are not prepared to waste the talents and abilities of so many Canadians just because they may be members of a group which, in the past, has suffered from discrimination.
To my mind, it is the mark of the kind of society in which we all believe that we truly provide for equality of opportunity, that we do not allow the weaker in our society to become still weaker, economically or socially, and that it is justified to have special measures to ensure that the economically weaker members of our society have an opportunity to improve their status.
Although I know there is some concern about the kind of approach employment equity will bring, I feel confident myself that if it is done in a sensible, reasonable kind of way, it will be truly to the benefit of our society.
How do you balance employment equity with our concept of a merit system? I do not think they are incompatible. We are

October 3, 1985
Employment Equity
still saying, with employment equity, that people have to have basic qualifications to do a job. We are not saying that unqualified people will be given jobs. We are saying that through adequate training opportunities people, who traditionally have been disadvantaged because they are part of minority groups, will now be given the appropriate consideration for employment opportunity.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, this legislation is result oriented. I think that is the only benchmark we should have in this kind of legislation.
We heard this morning, and I have also heard from other groups, that this legislation does not go far enough. Some people would say to us, "We want the full power of the state, whole new bureaucracies to force companies to hire people", but with that goes tremendous paper work and all sorts of things which, quite honestly, I do not think are very meaningful. You can have all sorts of bureaucrats running around with all kinds of reports and statistics, but when you get to the bottom line, the employer himself or herself has to understand the goals and objectives and has to make up his or her mind that a company is really committed to the program. It must not be a bunch of paper work being propounded by bureaucrats.
We also have to have the baseline data. Let me turn the attention of the House to Clause 4 of the Bill. I think this is the important section. Perhaps my colleagues on the other side of the House have missed the importance of this clause. It reads:
An employer shall implement employment equity by
(a)	identifying and eliminating each of the employer's employment practices, not otherwise authorized by a law, that results in employment barriers against persons in designated groups; and
(b)	instituting such positive policies and practices and making such reasonable accommodation as will ensure that persons in designated groups achieve a degree of representation in the various positions of employment with the employer that is proportionate to their representation
(i)	in the work force, or
(ii)	in those segments of the work force that are identifiable by qualification, eligibility or geography and from which the employer may reasonably be expected to draw or promote employees.
That is what this is really all about. First, you have to know what that data base is; how many employees there are in certain racial minorities, among the disabled, women and native Canadians for certain occupational categories from which you can draw. It is not a matter of saying that there should be 30 per cent women or 20 per cent of people with physical handicaps in this or that company. That is totally unrealistic.
What if I am running an operation in Toronto? We get the information and we know there are people with physical handicaps who have the basic qualifications or through training can achieve those qualifications. What if they make up 20 per cent of the potential workforce in a particular category? As a company, we will problably set a goal for ourselves. No goals can be set by legislation. Each employer in each geographic location, dealing with each kind of employment has to do that.
To me, that is the only rational and reasonable way you can go about implementing employment equity. All this talk about quotas and targets is a red herring. First, nobody wants quotas. Even Rosie Abella said, "No quotas".
Have you talked to women's groups lately?

I think the kind of approach that we are presenting in this Bill is workable. With the guidelines the Minister is putting forward, employers will understand how they can go about meeting the requirements of Clause 4 and putting them into effect.
Finally, let me speak about the comment on an enforcement mechanism that there is not a great policeman pounding on the door saying, "You have not achieved 20 per cent or you have not done this". But there is an enforcement mechanism. We have the Canadian Human Rights Commission, which already has the power in legislation to initiate complaints and initiative work. I do not think we need another bureaucracy to be the policeman. We have the highly respected Human Rights Commission, which is willing and able-
They can't make systemic changes in companies.

-and with the resources the Minister has already said will be made available to it, can do this effectively and bring about the enforcement as it is required under this Bill.
I am very confident that this Bill will provide the start we need to bring about employment opportunities for all sectors in our society that so badly need them. We recognize it as a start. We will see by the results what happens.
I see two possibilities. I see, and I hope it is a possibility, that through public education and public participation- because the Minister and her people will be working with employers, unions and target groups-we will achieve employment equity, and ultimately we will not need this legislation. I would like to see a sunset clause. I think that is the ultimate goal. In a way it is an interim measure to bring us up to those standards.
If I am wrong, if I am too optimistic, then perhaps we have to look at other measures. Personally, I do not think that that will be the way in which Canadians will respond to this legislation. Drawing from my own experience in the private sector, when the opportunity was given or the issue was drawn to the attention of the people with whom I worked, they were more than willing to make the accommodation and, with the assistance of the Minister and her officials, to help provide the mechanisms. I think there will be a very positive response throughout the country to this legislation.
Employment equity is not only a goal cherished by Utopian dreamers. It represents a fair approach toward equality and greater efficiency in the labour market. That is really the bottom line; all legislation has to be fair, and I believe this
October 3, 1985

legislation is just that. Also, I believe that an overwhelming majority of Canadians agree with us. The public will support employers who are making an honest attempt to promote equity in the workplace.
As I said, this is the first step. It is the beginning of a process of co-operation on the part of government, large employers, labour, and special interest groups for women, native people, visible minorities and disabled persons. Together we can show progress. The optimal use of our human resources constitutes an essential element of economic development. This legislation testifies to our commitment to social justice and economic renewal. All Canadians will welcome this long overdue step toward employment equity for all Canadians.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker in this period provided for questions and comments, I want to deal with three different areas. During my speech I raised the difference between the French text and the English text. Perhaps the Hon. Member opposite could explain why the English text indicates "Employment Equity" above Clause 4. I think that would pertain to everyone and to employment in general, not just to professionals. I realize that she talked about employment in general, but the French text indicates "equite professionnelle". Why is there a difference between the two texts?
Also the Hon. Member indicated that the goals and targets were unreasonable. If that is so, why did the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) make a very specific promise that we needed goals and targets in law? If they are unreasonable, why did he make that promise and why, now that the Conservatives are elected, did he break that promise?
Finally, she talked about our not knowing the legislation and she quoted Clause 4 of the Bill, which in part indicates that an employer shall implement employment equity, at least, that is what is indicated in English. It is somewhat different in French. In French it just urges employment equity. However, she did not talk about Clause 5 which tells us how that is to be done. Clause 5 indicates that it will be done through reporting, and that is spelled out in detail. It talks about reporting on how many employees there are in each sector or in each designated group, and so on. It indicates that employers must report about all of that.
If she looks closely at the Bill-and I am not sure whether she has read it-she will find that Clause 6 is the only part of it which deals with an offence. It indicates that it is an offence for these employer groups not to report to the Minister and states that there is a fine of up to $50,000. The only thing that is mandatory is the forcing of each group to report. On page 195 of the Abella Report, it was indicated that the court of public appeal was not good enough and that there had to be something mandatory. Why not make Clause 6 stronger and ensure that there are sanctions if a company fails to comply with employment equity? Why not do that? In Clause 6 there is only a sanction if it fails to report, and in Clause 7 the Minister has to lay a report before Parliament within a year or several months.
Employment Equity
Those are my questions. Why is there a difference between the French text and the English text? Does it only apply to professionals or does it apply to everyone? Why was there a campaign promise about targets and goals, if that Party did not mean targets and goals being mandatory or in the law? Finally, can the Hon. Member explain to the House how it is mandatory when the sanctions only apply to reporting, not to forcing a company to comply with the wishes and the words in the Bill? I agree that they are good words, good wishes and good sentiments, but only the court of public appeal enforces them. That is not good enough. The Minister should know that; she is an old-time politician.
Mr. Speaker, I object to my hon. friend saying that I might not have read the Bill. I think that is entirely uncalled for.
You said that about us.

Any Member of Parliament who has an intense interest in this subject, as I have had for 20 years, will have read the Bill thoroughly and understood it.
With regard to the French version, I am advised by my colleagues that equite professionnelle does indeed mean equity for all. I am sure, if there is any drafting misunderstanding, that this can be cleared up. Certainly the intention is that the meaning be the same in French as it is in English.
Turning to Clause 6, perhaps my hon. colleague might look at Subclause 5(2) in which it is indicated that a report under Subsection (1) shall be made in the prescribed manner. That manner will be outlined by the Minister in the regulations. It is not just that a report be made, but that the report be done in the prescribed manner. This will provide all the information about which we have been talking. It will have to show the data base upon which the employer obtained the information, how many women were in that geographic area and what their plans are to deal with them. All these things will be in the prescription set out by the Minister. It is not just that an employer can come along and put down a piece of paper. The report has to be done in the proper way. Perhaps my colleague might look at that in some detail.
As well, as the Minister and I have said, if these reports do not indicate that the employer is living up to the spirit of the legislation and if, for example, 60 per cent of the women were qualified according to the target qualifications and there was an obvious example that attempts were not being made to bring their own employment up to that, the Canadian Human Rights Commission will have that information, will be able to lay a complaint and conduct a thorough investigation. I really do not understand what more my hon. friend would ask for, other asking perhaps than policemen to go into places. That is not the kind of Government we want. We have perfectly adequate arrangements under this Bill to ensure that our intentions are honoured.

Mr. Speaker, I have a very short supplementary question. Why was the campaign promise of the Prime Minister not honoured that there would be targets and goals in

October 3, 1985
Employment Equity
legislation? Why was the promise made but not honoured? The Hon. Member seems to think honour is important.

Mr. Speaker, I dealt with that in my earlier discussion. Again, if we turn to Clause 4, it really deals with the concept. I do not know what the Hon. Member wants. Does he want us to put in place a piece of legislation that every employer will employ 40 per cent of a certain target group? The Hon. Member knows that that is ridiculous, that that cannot be put into a piece of legislation. This is the approach which is appropriate.
Why didn't you say that?
Because you are trying to take someone's words and put them in the wrong context. We are providing legislation which will enable people to implement employment equity fairly throughout the country.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member. Has she really discussed the Bill and the practices which the Government is applying, particularly the whole question of enforcement, with recognized women's groups, even with that government body, the National Advisory Council on the Status of Women? Those groups have certainly expressed considerable concern that there is not enforcement in the Bill. There is a requirement to report, but let us not forget that it is only for a few large companies. It is certainly not general throughout the federal jurisdiction, much less among those outside the federal jurisdiction. After the Hon. Member has answered that question, I have another one for her.

Mr. Speaker, I know the interests of my hon. colleague in this particular area and her work in this respect. I certainly respect that. We heard representations before the Standing Committee on Equality Rights from a number of groups representing women. Although they were dealing with a wide variety of issues, many mentioned concerns about this particular Bill, as I am sure they will when this Bill is before committee.
However I think, upon looking at this Bill and thoroughly understanding its relationship with the Human Rights Commission, that perhaps there has been some misunderstanding of how the two Acts together will provide an effective enforcement mechanism. I look forward to the opportunity of discussing this further with delegations from women's organizations.

Mr. Speaker, on the question of the Human Rights Commission, the Hon. Member and also the Minister have referred to this a number of times. The Minister in particular referred to it and I think the Hon. Member did also, from the point of view of equal pay for work of equal value. Judge Abella made the point that equal pay for work of equal value should be enforced as part of the employment equity policy. There is an Act now that allows individuals to make complaints to the Human Rights Commission. But what
women's groups are talking about-and I would certainly think that this is what Judge Abella was talking about-is systemic change, first within the Government and, secondly, within any Crown Corporations or any corporations that the Government does business with. This systemic change would ensure that women are not paid on a different basis than men for jobs of equivalent value. Women should not have to go on a case by case basis to complain-I wish the Minister would allow me to make my remarks without heckling. She sounds very defensive, I might say, Mr. Speaker. It is my belief that women should not have to go through all the trouble of getting their own legal documents and so on and go to the Human Rights Commission to appeal this on a case by case basis, that there should be requirements within legislation and within Government Departments as well that apply to companies that would change the system so there would not have to be these kinds of individual complaints.
She is way behind the times.

Mr. Speaker, I will have the opportunity perhaps of discussing this with my colleague more fully later on, but there is provision in the Human Rights Act for investigation into equal pay for work of equal value cases. 1 do not think it is really necessary to do that in this particular Bill. I know, from the discussions we have had with the commission, that it is are developing guidelines, as is Treasury Board, to have more implementation of that concept of equal pay for work of equal value within an establishment of an employer.
We want systemic change.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am very pleased with this opportunity to take part in the debate, but I am disappointed that I did not know until the very last minute that we would have this debate today. Nevertheless, I am happy to speak to this subject, and perhaps to reflect a little and report on the thoughts, wishes and comments of the groups we met while attending hearings of the Commission on Equality across Canada.
I can assure you, Madam Minister, that some of these groups will not be as delighted as you would wish them to be today because equality in the workplace, equal opportunity, equal access to the workplace were concepts they would welcome and which could be implemented through this legislation. It is unfortunate, but I do not think the legislation is going to be as successful as we would have liked.
That being said-

I would really like to suggest to you that it is a particular privilege to participate in the debate on the second reading of Bill C-62, an Act representing employment equity. The Bill, which results from the recommendations of the Abella Commission Report released last year, does represent a step forward. We have come some way from 1870 when the first two women were employed by the Public Service and from 1882
October 3, 1985

when the Toronto Labour Council first supported equal pay for equal work. We have come a long way from the concept of equal pay for equal work, and we have now moved into a concept to respond to systemic discrimination, which we call equal pay for work of equal value, which is a much fairer measure with respect to how we want to look at the society of today and tomorrow.
It has been a very long, hard struggle for these many groups-the women, the native people and the disabled-who have suffered from discrimination in the labour market and continue to be denied equal opportunity.
For them the goal of equality in real practical terms is still a distant goal and not yet realized. In the discussions leading up to the inclusion of Section 15, the equality section of the Canadian Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms, many expectations were raised that the disadvantaged groups in our society would finally achieve equal access to the labour market and that past injustices would be rectified. For these groups I believe the Minister's legislation has been a disappointment, and I say that in full awareness of what these groups have been saying to us we have criss-crossed the country. We thank the Minister of State for Immigration and Minister responsible for the Status of Women (Mr. McLean) who helped the special interest groups, that is the disabled, the visible minorities and the women's groups, with some financing so they could put their reports together for us. In essence, what they had to say in their reports was that perhaps there is a way that the legislation could be amended and moved forward so that the intent behind this legislation in all reality can be realized.
During the election campaign the Tories promised that they would implement an effective affirmative action program with adequate control, monitoring and evaluation mechanisms within the Public Service, its agencies and Crown corporations and that their Government would make clear to companies doing business with the federal Government that their performance in hiring and promoting women would be a key factor in obtaining contracts for goods and services. I would suggest that there are many, many companies which have less than 100 employees and which do business on a scale of less than $200,000 a year that really should be responding to the criteria that the Minister would like to see applied.
In the Throne Speech the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) stated, "Economic equality is the vehicle through which women will come to full partnership and participation with men in our society". These are laudable principles and are basically the reason the previous Liberal Government appointed Judge Abella to do the research and to set this commission in place so that it could find the reasonable avenues substantiated in fact that would indicate the route by which systemic discrimination could be removed.
I find that the present Government's commitment to all these recommendations has not been matched by its actions and, hopefully, that can be remedied en cours de route. Equality of opportunity takes many forms but the Government has not moved quickly to give clear federal leadership in this regard.
Employment Equity
I know that the Minister has said that this is the first step and that this is the first Government to undertake it. In some sense she is not incorrect. I would suggest that the groundwork was laid and the principles ahered to by the previous Government, but this present Government made promises that it did not live up to. I am saying to the Minister, amend the Bill and live up to those promises that were undertaken.
I think it is important to understand the steps that have to be taken to achieve the goal of equal access for disadvantaged groups. I would like to quote from a brief that was presented to the Equality Rights Committee by one of the members of the Citizens for Public Justice group. It reads:
We must make every effort to identify and remove, barrier by barrier, discriminatory advantages. The federal Government should set an example by further expanding its employment practices and decision-making processes so that all Canadians are not only free from adverse discrimination but, can also enjoy just employment conditions which provide fair access to meaningful work and equitable participation in the life of our society.
When we say we want every barrier and obstacle removed I would suggest that the record of today's employers does not indicate that they have voluntarily undertaken to remove the obstacles and to tear down the barriers. In this Bill, the employers are being given the responsibility to remove obstacles and take down barriers. I would suggest that we have to be more definitive in the description of the barriers and obstacles we want removed and have a measure that will relate specifically to the jobs which have in many instances unnatural and unnecessary qualifications that have nothing to do with the jobs in question.
As Judge Abella stated, employment equity is a strategy designed to obliterate the present and residual effects of discrimination and to open up equitably the competition for employment opportunities to those artitrarily excluded. It requires a special blend of what is necessary, that is fair and what is workable.
Affirmative action as a term refers to a comprehensive planning process for the elimination of systemic situations bringing about inequalities. We must now redress historic patterns of employment disadvantage suffered by designated groups. In an affirmative action program, the impact of employers' systems and practices is measured through an analysis of designated group employment within the organization and a realistic assessment of the number of target group members available in the labour market both in total and in the job and skill groups.
I know that the Hon. Member said that this falls under Clause 4 of the Bill. I would suggest that it is not substantive enough and it is left in the hands of the employers. I do not think that those steps to neutralize discriminatory practices include the kinds of goals and timetables necessary for achieving equitable representation of the designated groups within the organizations. I do not think they establish the kinds of remedial measures which will redress the past imbalances and make achievement of numerical goals possible.

October 3, 1985
Employment Equity
It is important to recognize that for many people, the term "affirmative action" has had negative connotations. It was for this reason, I believe, that Judge Abella coined the phrase "employment equity" but she expanded employment equity to include more than affirmative action. Even with the name having been changed, there is still some resistance to it as is obvious from the way this Bill has been applied.
The purpose of an employment equity plan is to open the competition to anyone who would be eligible for a position but for the existence of discrimination, unintentional or otherwise, and it does not mean that employers are mandated to hire unqualified persons. I think the opponents of these proposals tend to be uninformed about the many positive elements of such programs. Perhaps an education program for personnel departments would be very useful in helping them to undersand the implications of employment equity.
A review of the United States experience has shown that affirmative action programs have had a positive impact on the private sector, and although there was strong resistance at first, employers soon discovered that there was a wealth of talent that they had previously overlooked. Because of their past employment practices, they had restricted themselves to drawing from certain segments of society for their labour force. I think mandatory affirmative action laws showed that these disadvantaged groups could offer a pool of qualified people that could enhance and diversify workforces and bring new skills.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, in her conclusions, Judge Abella said that voluntary measures are an unsatisfactory response to the pervasiveness of systemic discrimination in the Canadian workforce and has therefore recommended that all federally regulated employers be required by legislation to implement employment equity. The key word here is "mandatory", and I do not agree with what the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) has said. There are no mandatory requirements in this Bill and I would suggest that the Hon. Member re-examine its contents. The intent should be made mandatory, but unfortunately the only thing that is mandatory is the reporting provisions and the fine of $50,000 for non-compliance. That will not help the disabled, the women and the visible minorities who pleaded before us for access under the kind of mandatory contract compliance that could be measured and examined in the light of reality.
It is important to note that this Bill is all about voluntary compliance, although there is mandatory reporting. If voluntary compliance had worked, that example would have been set a long time ago. However, it has not been set, and I believe it is very important to recognize that mandatory compliance has been absent from our legislation and businesses practices. Even the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, a group which advises the Government, has said that it wants the Government to go further than it has in its proposals to force Crown corporations and federally regulated companies to hire more women and minorities. The Council has examined the Bill in the light of mandatory requirements and has found it wanting as well.
Regarding the American experience, Victoria Smith, a senior consultant from New York, notes that business is comfortable with numerical goals and targets and that that is how business works. She indicated that she had just done surveys of her clients, most of whom are big Fortune 500 corporations, and of the 142 responses, 95 per cent indicated they would keep on using numerical goals to track the progress of women and minorities regardless of the Government's requirements because it is good, sound business. It is good for the corporation and it is good for the country.
Many groups have testified that voluntary compliance does not work. As Hon. Members well know, a right is only a right if it is enforceable. Otherwise it is just a lot of lovely words that mean nothing.
I think it is about time that the federal Government, its agencies, its Crown corporations and federally regulated sectors and companies doing business with the Government recognized the diversity of Canada's population and the potential of disadvantaged members. The cost of employment-equity programs has often been cited as an impediment to their implementation. However, the United States experience has shown that good use of human resources is just good business practice. Basically, we cannot afford not to apply good business practices in this highly competitive world in which we count on productivity as a bottom line.
Bill C-62 demonstrates that the Government has lacked the willpower and the leadership that is necessary to implement employment-equity programs effectively. I speak not only for myself but for all those groups that came before us with the feeling that the Minister would be applying the kind of regulations and laws that would have the impact that the Minister herself indicated they would. I am referring to the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, the Coalition of Provincial Organizations for the Handicapped and many groups belonging to the National Action Committee. They are all disappointed by the lack of an enforcement mechanism.
It is not enough for the Minister to say that public opinion will pressure companies and the Government to hire actively and to promote men and women from the targeted groups. Did she not read the chapter on enforcement mechanisms in the Abella Report? I believe she did and I am sure she studied it well.

I think the Minister should at least take another look at the following words: .. . "The obligation to implement employment equity" .. . which will remain just words if they do not have force of law. Ideally, enforcement should be entrusted to an agency that would be entirely separate from the Government. This agency would dispose of the necessary resources to fulfil its mandate, including competent staff with a good knowledge of labour relations, employment mechanisms and human rights issues.

Voluntary measures just do not work. Let us stop pretending that they do. Without goals and timetables, no measurable
October 3, 1985

differences can be noted. The Minister has spoken of criteria and guidelines for employment equity. I would like her to make these available so that we can all know on what premise she is working.
I would just like to remind the Minister that it is a good thing that my neighbour and confrere, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), fought and organized the fight to keep the census on line. The Minister knows that without the instrument to gather the date with which we can measure the base, the whole thing does not work. The question is: What is in the census questions? Do they meet the information needs? I hope the Minister will answer my questions in the affirmative because I wish as much as she that it works.
You have not read the legislation.

Yes, I have read the legislation. The Minister knows better than that. She knows that I would have read it and read it thoroughly.
The Minister has talked about criteria and guidelines for employment equity. I would like the Minister to make those available. In her job market strategy the Minister has indicated that employment equity will be an integral part of that. I believe that I read that provision correctly. Therefore, can the Minister provide us with her Department's goals and timetables for employment programs? In this way, in the future, the Canadian public can assess if the Government is setting the necessary examples for other sectors.
I would like to remind the Minister that in February, if my memory serves me correctly, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) announced that he had set up a joint committee with labour to review employment equity practices in the federal Government. The committee was to look into the matter of equal pay for work of equal value. He was to report back to us, but I have not heard from him yet. If I have missed his marvellous presentation, then I regret that. If I have missed it, I would like the whole of Canada to know where we have gotten to and what his report entailed, because equal pay for work of equal value is an integral part of the whole employment equity package, which the Minister has happened to overlook in her Bill.
Contract compliance, which is not covered in the legislation as I understand it, will be covered by regulation. I believe the Canadian public has a right to know if the Government and the companies with which it does business are complying with measurable goals and timetables. I recognize the need for flexibility in employment equity programs. I understand that small business and certain sectors need exemption under Section 1 of the Charter. However, that should not be used as a smokescreen for incomplete and insufficient data which are needed to provide an indicator of the success and the effectiveness of the measures taken.
I would now like to deal with the issue of sanctions. Clause 6 of the Bill would allow the Minister to impose a fine of
Employment Equity
$50,000 for failing to provide her Department with a report containing detailed information on employment practices. While this is not an insignificant amount of money, to say the least, it is not likely to improve the employment status of designated groups. The fact that Mr. Whoever-he-is had to pay a fine will not help the disabled. Nor will it help the minorities, or women, to find jobs. It will only prove he did not do his task.

and female employees employed in the same establishment who are performing work of equal value. Is the Hon. Member aware that this legislation exists? Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister for some of the clarifications which she has provided. However, I do have a few concerns which I would like to bring to the attention of the House. subsubtopic: TAX REBATE DISCOUNTING-OUTLAWING OF PRACTICE URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tax discounting is a service used mostly by low-income families. Indeed, two out of three persons who discounted their tax refunds reported a 1983 income of less than $8,000, and one out of three persons had incomes of less than $2,000. Therefore, the proportion of tax-filers who discount the most are at low income levels. Of the $41 million in refunds that were retained by the tax discounters, $15 million to $20 million was made up of child tax credits which are intended to help low-income families meet their needs.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) is aware of how important these child tax credit refunds are to low-income Canadians. They are used to buy furniture, household appliances, and children's clothing. The Minister is also aware that the tax system is being increasingly used as a vehicle for transfers to low-income Canadians. Poor families cannot continue to lose 15 per cent of their tax credits to discounters.
I would urge the Minister, therefore, to follow the recommendations of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs to take the necessary steps to outlaw tax rebate discounting or, at the very least, to adopt the position agreed upon in mid-September by the provincial Ministers
October 3, 1985

responsible for Consumer and Corporate Affairs to ban tax rebate discounting of the child tax credit.

subtopic: RESTRUCTURING OF INTERNATIONAL HARVESTER PLANT-EFFECT ON EMPLOYEES
RESTRUCTURING OF INTERNATIONAL HARVESTER PLANT-EFFECT ON EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some 300 workers at the International Harvester truck plant in Chatham, Ontario, are facing lay-offs as the company moves jobs and production to Japan. The company is phasing out its Cargo Star line, replacing it with a new modified version to be produced under contract with Nissan, beginning in 1986.
The Government has given much publicity to the inflow of foreign capital and jobs which its new open-door policy claims to have attracted. The Harvester case demonstrates the darker side of this open-door approach. The door swings both ways. This can create outflows of foreign capital and jobs as the multinational corporation restructures its global operations.
I urge the Government to investigate this Harvester move, and to bring in stronger Canadian content legislation to keep these jobs and production lines in Canada. The future of workers and communities like Chatham depends on such tough trade action.

subtopic: CANCELLATION OF OUR NATIVE LAND RADIO PROGRAM
CANCELLATION OF OUR NATIVE LAND RADIO PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the final broadcast of the radio program Our Native Land which has been cancelled by the CBC. I believe this decision on their part is wrong. Our Native Land provided natives in Canada with a means of communicating among themselves and with non-native Canadians for 20 years. A full-time production staff worked in Ottawa where decisions are made that affect native Canadians. Now a new team is in Toronto. This is wrong.
The leaders of the four national aboriginal organizations united to urge the CBC not to cancel the program. The CBC did not listen. Without Our Native Land there will be inadequate coverage of important events impacting on natives and of interest to non-natives.
Seventy thousand listeners per week knew that on Saturday they would hear stories about natives. The loss of a dedicated time slot means that they must listen to non-native public affairs programs and hope that there may be a story concerning their interests. This is unacceptable.
Natives today face many challenges that non-natives are interested in. For example, the 1987 First Ministers' Conference on Aboriginal Rights, the Task Force on Land Claims, review of funding for native programs and organizations, annual conferences of native, Inuit, Metis and Indian organizations, evolution towards self-government, community-based education and health services, and the cultural renaissance in native communities are all reasons why all Canadians need a regular native affairs program in a dedicated time slot. I urge the CBC to reinstate the program.

subtopic: ALLEGED TUNA PLANT TOUR-REQUEST FOR APOLOGY
ALLEGED TUNA PLANT TOUR-REQUEST FOR APOLOGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I refer to unfounded allegations by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), affecting myself and other members of the New Brunswick caucus in which he stated that we had prior knowledge of tainted fish from a New Brunswick cannery and that we had communicated that knowledge to the caucus and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
These allegations, whether direct or made as insinuations, have seriously affected the credibility of a number of Hon. Members, as well as their ability to carry on their functions as Members of this House.
The imputations of the Leader of the Opposition in my case and that of other New Brunswick Hon. Members are false and injurious. They are unfounded and without substantiation. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition has behaved irresponsibly by launching himself on a mud-slinging expedition on the theory that if enough mud is thrown some is bound to stick. On behalf of other members of our caucus, I protest against Parliament being used for tactics more worthy of the gutter. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition should withdraw statements that he cannot verify or substantiate. He should apologize to the New Brunswick Members of Parliament and to the Prime Minister. He should begin to conduct himself in a way worthy or the dignity of Parliament.
Members of Parliament cannot carry out their functions if they are to be subjected to unfounded allegations damaging their reputations by a person occupying the high position of the Leader of the Opposition. There should be an apology and a withdrawal by the Leader of the Opposition.

Mr. Speaker, while current employees of Canadian Pacific can bargain through their unions on many issues, including railway passes, the pensioners of CP cannot. They have no bargaining power and must rely on Members of Parliament in all Parties and Government to protect their rights and interests.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock, there were four minutes remaining in the question and comment period following the speech of the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone). I see that the Hon. Member is not present in the House at this time. Therefore, we will resume debate.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in my capacity as Minister Responsible for the Status of Women to address the implications of employment equity for the women of Canada. At the outset, I want to take a moment to congratulate my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), for her achievement with this Bill. She has conducted extensive consultations with all interested parties, consultations which give real meaning to this initiative. This is reflected in the successful drafting of the Bill, a document which is a bold first step. I am pleased and encouraged to hear Members opposite recognize the importance of this first step which represents a position which addresses the sensitive needs of both employers and target groups.
The employment equity legislation before us today ensures that no person will be denied employment opportunities or benefits for reasons unrelated to abilities. There is no doubt that such legislation is urgently needed in Canada. Despite a decade of voluntary affirmative action and equal opportunity programs, there has been little progress in the over-all economic advancement of women in the labour force.
As Members of the House will know, the statistics speak for themselves. Historically, the unemployment rate of women has always been higher than that of men. In 1982, women working full time full year earned only 64 cents for every dollar earned by men working full time full year.
The employment options of women are so narrow that fully three-quarters of employed women work in only five of 22 major occupations. Most of these jobs are not only low paying but are also dead-end jobs offering limited scope for advancement. In addition, many of these jobs are threatened by structural changes due to micro-electronics, automation and other technological developments. Further, many women who cannot find full-time jobs are forced to accept part-time work. In fact, in the year 1984, women accounted for 71 per cent of all part-time workers across our nation. This type of employment provides fewer jobs, fewer job benefits, less security and fewer promotion opportunities than full-time work.
Despite these roadblocks, the trend is such that women's participation in the labour force is growing. In the year 1974, the participation rate of women between the ages of 25 and 54 years was 48 per cent. A decade later in 1984, it had jumped to 66.7 per cent. It is estimated that by the year 1990, women will account for two-thirds of the labour force growth. Already over half of women whose youngest children are under three years old are now in the labour force.
Employment Equity
Another marked trend is the accelerated rate at which women are turning to self-employment. Women encounter specific barriers in this area of employment, particularly with regard to acquiring loans and financing credit. Although women's contribution to the formal economy as both employees and entrepreneurs has increased, women have not benefited equally. This must change.
Women workers are necessary and valuable contributors to the economy. Their full participation in the labour force is essential to ensure Canada's future growth. What we are proposing here is not merely justice but a part of our whole economic and job-creation thrust. The current under-utilization of women workers and their qualifications is a waste of human resources that Canada can no longer afford. As well, it results in conditions that women themselves cannot afford
I need not remind Hon. Members that women work for the same reasons men do: for their own personal satisfaction and to meet their own economic needs and those of their families. We know for a fact that if women did not work outside the home, over 60 per cent more families would be living below the poverty line. We know too that 85 per cent of all single-parent families are headed by women and that close to half or 47 per cent of these families live in poverty. Clearly, the inequities in our economic system and the social barriers that prevent women's full and equal participation in the economy cannot continue.
The employment equity legislation before us today brings together measures related to equal opportunity and affirmative action. It is designed to counter the restraints that keep women from attaining full parity with men in the labour markets. These constraints include economically limiting job segregation and occupational concentration, social attitudes which lead women to consider only a few types of occupations, systems which overlook significant numbers of trained and skilled women workers and the lack of training opportunities and upward mobility.
Members will recall that at the First Ministers' conference in Regina, the premiers committed themselves to improving access to training and child care in order to help women achieve economic equality. Some of the premiers at the Regina meeting have stated that they too are developing specific policy measures to implement employment equity.
Since we announced our response to the Report of the Commission on Equality in Employment last March, we have met with representatives of women's groups, business, labour, native people, disabled and the visible minorities to discuss employment equity. The swift introduction of employment equity legislation is further proof of our commitment to address this pressing situation.
The Government is setting an example in employment within its own jurisdiction. The federal Government, in strengthening its commitment to employment equity, will be seen to be a leader for provincial Governments and the private sector in supporting and promoting a structure of employment practice founded on merit and not on bias or barriers. We are doing so first for reasons of fundamental justice because

October 3, 1985
Employment Equity
barriers restricting the economic future of millions of Canadians must be removed. I also believe that employment equity is a practical measure leading to enhanced productivity and to economic prosperity. Employment equity measures will affect roughly one in five Canadian women. For the first time, the implementation of reporting of employment equity results will be mandatory and reported information will be available on the public record. Public scrutiny will be a valuable instrument of control, bringing pressure to bear for real progress. I have been encouraged by remarks made earlier in the debate by the Minister, the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) and Hon. Members opposite who have recognized the importance of data in addressing this sensitive situation.
The principle of employment equity is already established within the federal Public Service. As the employer, the Treasury Board is now working on a number of measures to ensure that this principle is further reflected in federal employment policies and practices. These include immediate initiatives to identify systemic barriers in the Public Service job classification system, intensified implementation of the Government's affirmative action program, with an added commitment for adequate resources. To assist the achieving of the stated goal Hon. Members will know that an invitation has been extended to the Public Service unions to participate in a senior level joint union-management committee to prepare a detailed implementation plan in the area of equal pay for work of equal value throughout the Public Service.
Employment equity measures are an integral part of the Government's economic strategy. Full participation by all Canadians contributes to economic growth. It ensures that our human resources are used to their fullest potential. A priority on jobs and economic renewal must involve an attack on barriers to equity, just as it must involve an attack on obstacles to growth. I believe that employment equity is both beneficial to women and fully compatible with the Government's principal economic priorities. Employment equity is not lip service to those Canadians who have been denied opportunities. Rather, I believe the legislation is a pragmatic program of action which will be the catalyst for change that will spread throughout all sectors of the Canadian economy.
As Minister responsible for the status of women I am aware of the particular systemic problems facing women in employment. For example, employment equity will help debunk outdated myths about working women. It will also alert employers to the cost incurred by overlooking qualified women. It will ensure that employers recognize the benefits to be gained by training, hiring and promoting women on the same basis as they do men. Employment equity is a bold new initiative. While it flows from the recommendations of the Abella Royal Commission on Equality in Employment, and while it is in keeping with the equality provisions of the Charter of Rights, it is as yet an innovative concept which will have to be tried and tested. Because of this we are endeavouring to take a flexible approach to the process of implementing employment
equity consistent with individual needs and the capabilities of employers involved.
There are some critics of the legislation and we have heard their comments echoed in the debate thus far. There are those who say the legislation is inadequate, weak, impassive or vague. Others, at the opposite end of the spectrum, charge this is government interference, undue coercive measures, bureaucratic nightmares, regulations or what have you. Yet, the Government's commitment to employment equity is firm and unyielding. We realize that the current under-utilization of women, native Canadians, visible minorities and disabled persons in the labour force is a waste of human resources which Canada can no longer afford. We are determined to involve Canadians fully in the economic renewal and in the life of this nation. The full participation of these groups is essential to ensure our country's future economic growth.
Results are what matter and results are what we are seeking to achieve. Interestingly enough, in her report, Judge Abella encouraged the Government to see that the legislation looked to results rather than regulations. I reiterate that the voluntary approach of the previous Government had very limited success, as Members opposite have recognized in the debate. It is only through legislated, mandatory requirements that we are likely to bring about real employment equity.
Examples of similar mandatory programs which have worked in Canada are the French language program in the federal Public Service, which raised Francophone representation to the same proportion as the over-all Canadian membership, and the preferential hiring of World War II veterans. These two measures were imposed on the system, backed by significant political will, and they yielded positive measurable outcomes.
We ask in 1985 no less for other target group members in our society: women, native people, handicapped persons and visible minorities. Our commitment to this principle of employment equity is on the record.
There is a potential of 1,000 companies employing close to one million workers who will be affected by the legislation. Instead of perceiving employment equity as an obstacle to economic growth, we must realize there are benefits to be gained, not only by the target groups but by employers and the economy as a whole when we promote sound, fair human resource planning-a structure of employment practices founded on merit. In fact, the principles of employment equity go to the very heart of rejuvenated Canadian economy. Canadian economic renewal requires the full participation of all members of the community.
Up to this point in the debate we have been encouraged by the response that this legislation is a step in the right direction. Earlier in the debate the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) indicated that while in the committee stage he wishes to explore some aspects, he and others in his Party see it as a step in the right direction. In response to the concerns raised by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) with respect to the fact that somehow equal pay is not in force and is not related, we wish
October 3, 1985

to remind Hon. Members that this is already in place in the federal jurisdiction but not, of course, in many of the provinces.
Others have been concerned that the provisions are not voluntary. I wish to suggest that not only will public opinion be brought to bear through mandatory reporting mechanisms but that there is the commitment of the Government to strengthen, as necessary, the Human Rights Commission in order to undertake this action.
Earlier in the debate it has been underlined that in order to move forward with this step we require the data. Other than making a bureaucratic effort, what we wish to do is have the companies come back and show us what they are doing to give us that data. We want to assure the House that there will be provisions for enforcement and that there will be in the regulations a number of the concerns addressed which have been raised.
The Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) raised a matter which I thought was most important and one on which I would like to encourage suggestions. That was the concern for educational programs, the need for target groups and the importance of this to Canadians. I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that as this legislation moves forward we, as Hon. Members of this House, might be part of that educational program on behalf of women. We might see, as a part of this exercise with employers and employees, that there is an essential educational ingredient for all Canadians.
I am confident that the Government can achieve the goals outlined in this legislation. This legislation can have a meaningful impact on the lives of all members of the designated target groups so that economic equality will be within their grasp. Employment equity legislation clearly spells out the Government's intention to create true equality of opportunity for those who have not enjoyed this right previously. This legislation will go a long way toward ensuring that all Canadians will be able to share the benefits of future economic growth. We look forward to the support of Hon. Members on all sides of the House for this first and historic step in beginning to address these longstanding inequalities and in opening up this truly great opportunity for resource development within Canada.

speechtext:
It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 46, to inform the House that the questions
Employment Equity
to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria)-The Administration-(a) Request for review of contract awards (b) Conflict of interest guidelines; the Hon.
