The House resumed consideration of the motion of Miss MacDonald that Bill C-62, an Act respecting employment equity, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in the remarks of the Minister, and I have a number of questions which I would like to ask him. The Minister said that the Government is adopting a flexible approach consistent with the needs and abilities of the employers. I hope I have quoted him correctly. I would like to ask him if this is not really what the Liberals were saying as well. When the Liberals were in Government, and we were on this side, along with the Conservatives, we were both extremely critical of the Liberal Government because it was saying that we must be flexible. It backed down on mandatory contract compliance, for example, and said, "We'll leave it to the business people to establish their own ideas of what is right". The Government really shied away from the issue.
It seems to me that really the Conservative Government is doing the same as the Liberal Government in trying to use just persuasion and a very flexible approach which has no teeth in it. no "mandatory enforcement" and I insist we use that term because that is really what it means.
Second, the Minister also said that this was a step in the right direction. I would like to ask the Minister why we should only take a step in the right direction. If we are going to do something which is so important and, as the Minister said, which will ensure that no person will be denied employment for reasons other than ability, why should we not go all the way? Why should we only be making this a data collection project? Why should we not be establishing a goal? Why should there not be a mechanism outside of the employer himself which establishes the goals and then enforces these goals? Why do we need to take so much time about it? It will be at least 10 years before the Human Rights Commission can

October 3, 1985
Employment Equity
get back to the employers to criticize any changes. It will take that long to get the information together and then to try to do something about it. I would really like to leave those two questions with the Minister.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for her comments and assure her that those concerns have been addressed. The Hon. Member raised three items. With respect to the question of flexibility, I want to suggest to the Hon. Member that, as she will recall, the Abella Commission recommended that the Government take a flexible approach-
It recommended enforcement.

-and recognize the diversity of the country and the diverse needs of the employing sector. Second, the Hon. Member speaks of mandatory enforcement. I want to remind her, and the House, that this Bill does have within it mandatory provisions, mandatory for employment equity, mandatory for reporting, and these are legal tools-
Reporting but not change.
Tell us what is being done.

I suggest to the Hon. Member that she read Clause 4 of the Bill and the comments of the National Action Committee, and others. I understand, as does the Hon. Member, the sense of urgency on the part of the women's movement in relation to this Bill. I am interested to see that the women's movement endorsed Clause 4 which states, and I quote:
An employer shall-
-not "may". In my understanding of the English language, "shall" implies mandatory-
How are you going to do it? It's fine to put the words down.
In answer to the comments of the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville in the debate this morning, we talked about the importance of regulations.
Its mandatory manipulation.

The Hon. Member also spoke about the question of the next steps to be taken. I agree with her entirely. What we are hoping for is that, for example, the Province of Manitoba will follow and join in. This is not something the federal Government can do on its own. What we are trying to do is deal within our own jurisdiction.
But you're not dealing with it. You're just taking statistics.

What we are also trying to do is to set an example in front of the Canadian private sector, the unions and the provinces with the hope that they will begin to follow it. I would like to also reiterate that in the report of Judge Abella, she spoke about the importance of having legislation which was "results oriented", which would not bring back
reports from employers which, somehow, do not reflect what is happening but is their way of getting around the regulations. We have here a mechanism in the Human Rights Commission to see that those reports are acted upon, as against the alternative of companies having plans which would have to be approved with more regulatory imposition and fines and so on.
In response to the Hon. Member, I suggest that the concerns she is addressing are concerns which are very much in front of the Government. This is a first step. I remind the Hon. Member that five years ago this was not on the agenda at all and while many quite obviously would wish that there was more in the first step, we make no apologies for coming forward with mandatory provisions, for taking the first step. We will be acting with Crown corporations, with contracts through the Department of Supply and Services, and I believe this Bill will become a complementing part of our action toward a total comprehensive program in relation to justice for target groups.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to characterize the Government's Bill not as flexible, but as flaccid in that it does nothing on a mandatory basis to determine that Crown corporations and the federal Government comply on pay equity issues like affirmative action. Is it not a little embarrassing for his Ministry responsible for the status of women-and I know he sees his wife as more than a rose in his lapel-to be in the same Government which, since the introduction of the new Conservative mandate, has decided that the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation will no longer pay for renovations to make apartments accessible for the disabled? On the one hand, Crown corporations and the federal sector are being told to make a plan to make employment accessible to women, minorities, and the disabled. On the other hand, through the Minister's own Ministry, the Government is cutting back on the issue of accessibility which is obviously critical to those people who will be able to compete in the employment market.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member raises an issue which is tangential to this particular issue. On the matter of action in this area her Party was not evident over the last number of years with any legislative measures whatsoever. On the matter of sensitizing and education about target groups, let me also remind the Hon. Member that in the last few week the House established a standing committee on the condition of disabled persons.
On the question of education and sensitizing all of our instruments, I would invite her to join with me and others in the Government. Our positions in relation to equality for target groups, be they women or the disabled, are clear. We now need my commitment as the Minister responsible to encourage and work with my colleagues in Cabinet to see that we integrate those concerns into all of our planning processes. As we are able, despite the limited resources that may be available, we must ensure that these groups are targeted as special groups with special concerns. As was indicated earlier in the debate, education in all aspects is important so that
October 3, 1985

when decisions are made the issues of accessibility and the needs of the disabled will be front and centre. This Bill puts that in front of the entire Government as well as the entire community.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The period for questions and comments is now over. Resuming debate, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell).

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased, as the New Democratic critic for the status of women, to be speaking on this Bill this afternoon. As we have already indicated, Mr. Speaker, we feel that this is very weak legislation. We agree with the intended thrust of it, but we feel that it is very weak. In fact, I would say that it is mush.
As I said, we support the goal of the Bill which is to bring about true equality in the workplace for women, for physically and mentally handicapped people, for visible minorities, and for natives. However, there are very fundamental flaws in Bill C-62 which will, we believe, prevent the achievement of this goal. Organizations which represent all four sectors are extremely dissatisfied in most cases and would agree with most of the reasons. The Minister said this morning that it will enshrine equality in the workplace and that it ensures access to opportunity for all Canadians. Those are pretty grand goals and I only wish that they could be implemented. I am sure that the Minister sincerely wants to do this, but I have very serious concerns that this is not achievable through this legislation.
The legislation calls only for a reporting of workplace data related to the four groups. It imposes a fine if the designated employers do not complete this report within five years. The reporting is mandatory, but that is only a first step. This legislation does not require the establishment of objective goals set by someone other than the employer, targets, or a timetable for employing members of the designated groups in a much fairer proportion. In other words, there are no real targets, and certainly no quotas.
There is no enforcement mechanism to require compliance by employers, no monitoring agency, and no penalty if the employer does not make changes. I find it hard to understand why there is a fairly stiff penalty if they do not report, but there is no penalty if the employer does not make changes. It is difficult, of course, to impose penalties if you do not know what those changes are going to be. The Bill applies only to selected employers. The Ministers said that it would affect everyone, but in reality it applies only to approximately 500 of the largest corporations in the federal sector. Maybe there is hope for a trickle-down effect, but I think this would be wishful thinking. As well, the time allowance for employers to make changes is far too lengthy. As I understand, it will take three years to compile the first report and another three to five years to study the results. What will happen after that? By then the Government could be changed.
Employers are left to make whatever changes they deem to be reasonable. This whole Bill is so subjective. It is nice to try to get employers to be more progressive and to care more about equal representation in employee groups, but they have
Employment Equity
a very vested interest. Many of the American business people who were quoted this morning said that they feel that mandatory affirmative action really works. They like it and feel it is productive from a business point of view as well as a human point of view. I do not understand why we have not put more teeth into this Bill.
The Minister said that we will use the force of public opinion. Of all people on the Government side, the knows through her fight for equality that women have never really achieved very much through the force of public opinion. I would think that disabled people, natives, and visible minorities have even less of a chance of achieving this through public opinion. Simply because an employer may feel a little embarrassed is not going to change the whole scheme of things.
As well, the Bill includes no reference to equal pay for work of equal value. According to the experts in this field, equality in employment must include equal access to jobs and equal pay for work of equal value. There is not much point in getting a job if you do not have a fair rate of pay. Judge Albella and all other authorities on affirmative action agree that any plan must include a requirement that employers will practise equal pay for work of equal value. Judge Abella has said that it is not enough to get women and minority groups into jobs, they must be paid fairly according to the value of that job compared to similar jobs.
We know, as the Minister pointed out this morning, that there is equal pay for work of equal value legislation. We all know that there is human rights legislation, but the Minister herself admitted that this has not been enforced and has not worked. We know that this is partly due to lack of staff, but it is more than that. Women still have to prepare complaints and go on a case-by-case basis to the Human Rights Commission. Members will recall that it was two years before the Bell employees were even heard. Many women do not have the ability, the time, or the expertise to prepare their case. They might not even know that this was their right. Therefore, there has not been adequate enforcement of equal pay for work of equal value.
This Bill is an opportunity for the Government to strengthen that principle. Government employers, whether it be Crown corporations or the Government itself, should be required by this legislation to practise that principle. The onus must be on the employer to make systemic changes, it should not left to a woman to complain individually or the Human Rights Commission to wait for complaints. This should be part of the agreement made with every employer involved in employer equity and I urge the Minister to look at this again.
We have looked at it.

I am not convinced the Minister has done that at all. I think the experts in the field would say the same thing, including Judge Abella.
The sixth point I want to make is that the Bill ignores the important role of collective bargaining. Last week I attended a

October 3, 1985
Employment Equity
special conference held by the Canadian Labour Congress. Well over 500 representatives of trade union affiliates were there and expressed great concern about this Bill. The Government has not included in the Bill the importance of referring to the collective bargaining role which is of great concern to these groups. The Minister has already presented some facts regarding the deplorable situation facing women in the job market, a situation which has not improved. We hope very much that this legislation, if it can be improved and toughened, will help women as well as other designated groups.
I would like to make reference to the comments of some other people regarding this Bill. Judge Abella, of course, cannot comment on the legislation but she said that voluntary compliance does not work. There must be an enforcement agency, that is very clear from her remarks. The Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women is a Government recognized agency which is supposed to be advising the Minister responsible for the Status of Women. Obviously he has not been taking their advice because he did not refer to their points at all. They said they were very disappointed that crucial elements in Judge Abella's recommendations are absent from the Government's proposal, such as the lack of a mechanism to provide co-ordinated and effective enforcement of employment equity. There are other groups I could refer to, Mr. Speaker, but my time is getting short and I want to introduce a very important document into the record this afternoon. I will be glad to see that the Minister gets a copy of this. It was compiled by the CLC and compares the key Abella Report recommendations with this Bill and also refers to the CLC position on affirmative action, a term they prefer to use regarding this same issue.
The first point they make is that Judge Abella said that all federally regulated employers should be required to implement employment equity. The two key words are "all" and "required". Bill C-62 says that federally regulated employers and Crown corporations employing 100 or more are required to implement employment equity.
That is right, "required".

The CLC feels that legislation at both federal and provincial levels must make it mandatory for employers to negotiate programs with unions. I hope the Minister will have another look at that.
The second point is that the legislation should require employers to implement a program of filing data, et cetera- this is Judge Abella speaking-and an enforcement mechanism must be implemented. Bill C-62 requires that employers implement a program and file reports. The programs require no approval and there is no enforcement mechanism other than the filing of the reports to be made public. The CLC of course agrees with the Abella Report recommendations.
As well, Judge Abella says that discriminatory barriers should be eliminated. The Bill requires that employment barriers be identified and removed. Those are fairly similar. The fourth point was that employers should be required to have employment equity committees consisting of representatives of
management, labour and the designated groups. There is no legislated requirement for committees, so that is another point we will want to look at. The CLC has strongly recommended equal representation by union and management on any committee and the union should select its own representatives. Judge Abella said no quotas should be imposed and the Bill says no quotas or targets will be imposed. The CLC says targets and timetables must be set to ensure progress. Judge Abella says employers must be given flexibility, as the Minister mentioned earlier, and the Bill gives total flexibility to employers. The CLC says that unions must have the right to negotiate changes into collective agreements, including employment practices and procedures.
They are not very willing to do so.

Judge Abella says there is an obligation to file data but the requirement to implement employment equity should take effect immediately. I think that is quite different from what this Bill requires. It requires that employers shall commence filing reports on June 1, 1988, and once a year thereafter. They will begin to implement employment equity in 1985 and they will submit plans to Treasury Board. The CLC feels there should be regular reporting to an enforcement agency. Judge Abella says that the enforcement of employment equity requires an independent agency with sufficient resources, qualified staff and an ongoing consultative relationship in the development of guidelines with business, labour and designated groups. That is not the type of enforcement agency included in this Bill. There will be complaints that can be lodged with the Human Rights Commission but we do not feel this is effective. The enforcement of change is what has not really been dealt with.
The CLC feels there must be strong penalties for non-compliance and impartial boards to adjudicate disputes. The Abella Report says that contract compliance should be imposed by legislation. This could include specific goals and timetables. There are no goals and timetables in this Bill. The report says that equal pay for work of equal value should be part of all employment equity programs and more resources should be allocated for enforcement.
I could go on and mention the other matters which are not covered at all and which are so important to women. It is not enough to have open access to jobs; they must be jobs at fair rates of pay with opportunity for promotion. More than that, in many cases women cannot move up if they do not have child care, adequate training, including pre-employment training, which will help them to be competitive with traditionally male dominated occupations. We feel that changes are needed to this Bill. I hope very much that there will be a chance to make some of those changes through amendments, but, as the Minister responsible for the Status of Women said, it is only just a step. It is not a big step, and there are serious omissions in the Bill.
October 3, 1985

Mr. Speaker, does the Hon. Member realize that she just blew her case when she quoted the analysis of the CLC about this Bill? She stated that CLC indicated that the Bill required employers to implement employment equity. The CLC recognizes, as do we, that the Bill requires employers to implement employment equity. That is mandatory, but it does not do it for small business. CLC recognizes that the mandatory action is in Clause 4 of the Bill wherein employers are required, by law, to implement employment equity. Is the Hon. Member aware of that?
Was she aware, when she talked about flexibility, that Judge Abella indicated in her report that it would also be expected that employers would set annual internal objectives, that these would not be required by statute and that no quotas would be imposed? I think the Hon. Member tried to leave the impression that the recommendations of the Abella Report were not being followed. We have followed them in very many cases, particularly the section concerning enforcement mechanisms. Judge Abella recommended four models of consideration by the Government. Is the Hon. Member aware that the fourth model as an enforcement mechanism relied upon the provisions already in effect in the Canada Labour Code and upon the Canadian Human Rights Commission? That is the agency which we chose as the mechanism to ensure the accumulation of data. Does she realize that the Canadian Human Rights Commission, under Article 32(3), has been given the right to initiate a complaint? It has not been able to do that so far. It has never used that particular part of the legislation because it has not had data available to enable it to do so. This legislation makes that possible. Does the Hon. Member realize that?
Finally, when the Hon. Member talks about timing, does she realize that the moment this legisation is passed, employment equity goes into effect? Companies will have 1986 within which to develop their plans and methods. They have to begin counting the data as of January 1, 1987, and reporting on that full year by the beginning of 1988. From the moment the Bill is passed, there is an onward march which leads companies to the development of their plans in 1986, to the implementation of their plans in 1987 and to the reporting on those plans in 1988. If that process is not carried out, they will be subject to the penalties in the Bill. Does she realize those things?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I realize what is in the Bill. Of course the Minister does not agree with the criticisms I have been making about the very things which she stated. It is one thing to say that employers "shall" implement employment equity. However, how will they do that? As I understand it, it is really being left up to them to gather the data and, if they do not gather the data, there will be a penalty. However, what will they do with the data? That is left up to them, as I understand it. The Minister can correct me if I am wrong, but it is up to them to establish what is employment equity in their case. How many native people should they employ? How many women should they employ and in what kinds of jobs? How many disabled people or people of a visible minority
Employment Equity
origin should they employ? My point is that the onus is on the employers to establish their own targets and goals. It is unreasonable and unfair, in a way, to leave that up to employers.
This morning it was indicated that many business people in the United States like mandatory affirmative action. They like to be told what has to be done, and there have been positive results from this requirement. 1 cannot understand how employers can establish their own targets and how we can be reassured that it will result in an effective systemic change which will provide equal opportunities for the groups 1 have mentioned.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister left me rather dismayed because she did not admit that the Bill was a weak one. She talked about an enforcement mechanism involving the Canadian Human Rights Commission. I have searched in vain throughout the entire Bill, and the Canadian Human Rights Commission is not in fact mentioned as the enforcement agent. She talked about how this would bring employment equity into the workplace right away, yet went on to agree that reporting was not meant to begin until 1988. Reporting to Parliament will not begin until this time three years hence. An employer who was challenged to that point would certainly say: "We will have to get this under way", but we are talking about some time in the life of the next Parliament. For example, we are talking about a situation where a woman aged 21 in the workplace today would be 24, 26 or 27 before any conceivable action might occur.
Also the Hon. Minister talked about the Abella report. 1 will refer to page 195 of that report and ask the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) to comment on it. Judge Abella indicated that a voluntary program with a mandatory reporting requirement was nonetheless voluntary in the absence of a requirement to remedy the discrminatory practices disclosed by the information reported. The penalty in the Bill for not reporting is heavy, but there is no penalty for doing nothing. The only penalty is for failing to report that nothing was done.
Also Judge Abella indicated that a requirement of public reporting may result in public pressure on a company to revise its systems, but that it was unrealistic to rely on public opinion as an effective monitoring agent. She went on to indicate that it would result in a speculative and scattered approach and would create the perception, in the absence of enforcement, that the issue was deserving on only casual attention.
When affirmative action on a voluntary basis was tried in Ontario, barely 200 firms out of tens of thousands actually did anything in a concrete way. Does the Hon. Member expect that much more will result from the Bill at the federal level?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the elaboration of my colleague, particularly his references to Judge Abella regarding the absence of any requirement to remedy a discriminatory situation. Again I say to the Minister that that is obviously what is lacking here. I agree completely with the comments about public opinion, that public opinion is not

October 3, 1985
Canada Pension Plan
really the way to bring about change and to require it in an authoritative mandatory manner.
I am not from Ontario, but aside from having very fine reports at the end of three years and perhaps a few fines if reports are not submitted, I would certainly be very skeptical about the Bill bringing about the major change urgently needed for the affected groups.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a comment. I think we are taking a very major step forward today as a maturing nation. It is not the end of the road, as some Hon. Members have indicated. We certainly know which route we want to follow. I, for one, congratulate the Hon. Minister. She has worked tirelessly in this area, month after month, year after year, to develop job opportunities and equality programs which all her Liberal predecessors did not put together in the last 15 years.

speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Rodriguez (Nickel Belt) moved
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-247, an Act to amend the Canada Pension Plan (survivor's pension) be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, may I at the outset say that I would certainly want to participate in the question of order involving this particular Bill. I have no reservations about the fact that it is a Bill that is properly introduced into the House and should be properly debated.
The purpose of Bill C-247 is to eliminate discrimination on the basis of age from the Canada Pension Plan. A person in receipt of disability benefits under the plan should have the assurance that in the event of his or her death the surviving
spouse and dependants will receive whatever benefits are left in the Plan irrespective of the age of the spouse.
At the moment if the spouse is 35 years of age or younger, that spouse cannot collect the survivor's benefits under the Canada Pension Plan Act. I intend to prove that this is an unfair provision in the Act, that in fact the surviving spouse of any age should be able to collect the pension. The Act provides that people start contributing to the Canada Pension Plan at age 18. Therefore, if a person starts contributing to the Canada Pension Plan, providing they meet the basic requirements, which is six years contributions in the last 10 for a disability pension, it seems to me that providing they meet those particular criteria then they should be able to collect the survivor's pension irrespective of the age of the spouse.
I suggest and argue that the law is an arbitrary one. What is so magical about the age 35? Why not 25, or 45, or 30 or 46? The very arbitrariness of picking a number, it seems to me, is not a fair way in which to administer a pension scheme.
I know from my own experience that many workers, because so many of them work in the mines, become disabled at very young ages and many of them pass on as a result of accidents in the mine. Their spouses, of which 99.9 per cent are women, are unable to collect yet they may have families, have no income and are unable to collect the survivor's benefits from the Canada Pension Plan.
That seems to me to discriminate against them not only because of age but, because of the nature of the occupation, it discriminates against them because they are women. 1 would refer to Section 15(1) of the Charter of Rights under the section of equal rights, and I quote from Section 15(1):
Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.
Clearly, Section 44(1 )(rf) of the Canada Pension Plan Act is unconstitutional and is outlawed by the Charter of Rights and the equality rights section, Section 15(1). We cannot have a law that contravenes what we now hold as a basic right of Canadians. We cannot discriminate based on age.
The Canada Pension Plan is a plan to which employers and employees contribute. Nine million workers at the present time pay 1.8 per cent of their yearly salary, up to a maximum of $379.80, into the Plan and their employers pay the same. Self-employed people pay the full $759.60 themselves.
The Canada Pension Plan has been accumulating considerable sums of money which the federal Government in turn has loaned back to the provinces for very small rates of return. Indeed, it is estimated that the provinces would never be able to pay back to the Canada Pension Plan the money they owe. Now we have a movement afoot to get workers and employers to put a greater percentage of their income into the Canada Pension Plan. The scenario is simply that the Canada Pension Plan would have larger amounts of money to once again lend to the provinces.
October 3, 1985

This particular change that I am proposing is not guaranteed to put the Canada Pension Plan into the red. It is not an amendment that encroaches upon the Treasury of Canada. The Canada Pension Plan is the fund into which employers and employees contribute. The Government of Canada does not contribute a penny. My amendment does not encroach upon the federal plan. These are moneys which the Canada Pension Plan program administers. It is money contributed by employers and employees.
I would argue that my amendment is a reasoned one. It conforms to Section 15(1) of the Canadian Constitution, 1981, the equality rights section of the Charter of Rights. It seems to me that it is only fair that the surviving spouse of anyone who is on a disability pension under the Canada Pension Plan Act should receive the survivor's pension irrespective of what age he or she may have attained, whether it is 29 or 34 or what it is.
Right now I am dealing with the case of a widow from my riding who missed the cut-off of 35 years because her thirty-fifth birthday was three days away.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Got to have a cut-off.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
That is right. That is a very smart response from the Tory benches. Ministers can trot around Europe at great cost to the taxpayers. The Government can bail out a bank for $1 billion. We can talk about restraint while the Ministers spend taxpayers' money like drunken sailors. She said she spent three days in bed when she was supposed to be out doing Government business.
It is all right for well-heeled Tories to talk about cutting people off. However, we do not have to cut them off. The plan is funded. The contributors are paying their fair share for this kind of coverage. The only reason the money is not there is because we have been lending it to the provinces. Now we are going to have the contributors contribute an even greater percentage to the Canada Pension Plan.
This amendment is fair. It will bring some equity and fairness to the Canada Pension Plan Act of 1966. It will eliminate the arbitrariness built into Section 44(1)(6) of the present Act. It seems that it is only just that the surviving spouse of someone who was collecting a disability pension under the Canada Pension Plan Act should indeed receive a survivor's pension.
I may also point out that things are fine for those who live in urban communities in which there are lots of opportunities for employment, particularly for women. However, in areas like mine, predominantly a mining community, once a spouse dies, the survivor hopes to collect the survivor's pension because there is no possibility for the spouse to step out of mourning and into a job. It is just not possible. That is why the spouse who was working was contributing to the plan. He was paying for this kind of coverage. The plan includes a death benefit, a disability provision and a pension at age 65.
Canada Pension Plan
An exception was made in the Act. The present Act indicates that if a surviving spouse is under 35 there is only one way that she can collect the pension and that is if she is disabled. I do not think that those who framed the Act in the first place were aware of the difficulties they created for a person who worked in a mine, was injured, received a disability pension and then passed away leaving his spouse unable to collect the pension because she was under age 35. Children may be involved and there is no opportunity for employment. It is a fund to which the spouse contributed and from which the surviving spouse is entitled to collect.
I call on Hon. Members to support this very reasoned, fair and just amendment. I call for the support of Bill C-247.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am very pleased indeed to be able to speak to this amendment to the Canada Pension Plan Act proposed by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez). I think all of us in this House realize the importance to our whole pension structure of the Canada Pension Plan. I must commend the Hon. Member for making an attempt to improve the Canada Pension Plan.
We all know or should know that our pension system works on three main tiers. First there is the tier composed of the Canada Pension Plan, the Old Age Security and the GIS, all government programs. The second tier is composed of the industrial and company pension plans and the third tier is composed of personal savings including RRSPs, homes, cars and bank accounts. Those three things are all forms of assistance for which people can plan during their working lives so they may have an adequate pension when they retire.
For most people in Canada, there is no doubt that the Canada Pension Plan and the OAS are the main supports for retirement. That is why I commend the Hon. Member for attempting to make some improvements to these plans. However, I would like to correct some misunderstandings with which he may have left the House while he spoke. The wording of his amendment is liable to cause some difficulty in determining what he said.
From the wording of the motion, one could be given the impression that the Canada Pension Plan survivor benefits are paid only to the surviving spouse of a person who was in receipt of a CPP benefit when he or she died. This, of course, is not the case. I am sure the Hon. Member knows that but that is not clarified by the wording of the amendment.
We should know that CPP benefits are paid to the surviving spouses of deceased contributors who, on their death, met the minimum contributory requirements. What are these requirements? Specificially, benefits are paid to survivors of contributors who have made contributions for at least three years and for one-third of the period during which he or she could have made contributions for 10 years, whichever is less. Further, as the Hon. Member mentioned, if the deceased spouse satisfies these minimum requirements, the surviving spouse must also meet certain conditions. She must be 35 years or older or, if she is not 35 years or older, then she must be disabled or have dependent children. Only when the deceased had made suffi-

October 3, 1985
Canada Pension Plan
cient contributions and the surviving spouse meets one of the eligibility criteria to which I referred does entitlement to a CPP survivor's benefit exist.
If eligibility is determined, then the amount of the benefit to be paid is calculated, once again taking the survivor's age or presence of a disability or dependent children into account. The amendment proposed by the Bill before us suggests that survivor benefits be paid to a surviving spouse under the age of 35 years. Currently, this survivor would be entitled to a benefit only if he or she was disabled or had a dependent child. However, what level of benefit does the Member suggest? I think it would be very relevant in terms of the costs to workers to know the amount of the benefits. The Hon. Member has not mentioned this. The reason I ask this question is because the way the current benefit levels are determined is rather complicated.
Under the current plan, the level of survivor benefits payable is also dependent on age. For instance, survivors over the age of 65 receive 60 per cent of the deceased spouse's retirement pension which was paid or which would have been paid at the time of death had the deceased reached the age of 65. For survivors under the age of 65, the survivor's benefit is composed of two parts. First, there is a flat-rate component of $87.56 per month as of 1985 and an earning-related component equal to 37.5 per cent of the deceased contributor's retirement pension which was paid or which would have been paid had he or she been entitled to receive it. The maximum monthly earnings related component payable in 1985 is $163.28 for a total maximum survivor's pension of $250.84. However, it should be noted that not all eligible surviving spouses under age 65 receive this level of benefit. For example, a surviving spouse between the ages of 35 and 45, who is not disabled or who has no dependent children in his or her care, receives a benefit which is reduced by one one-hundred-and-twentieth for each month he or she is under the age of 45 at the time of the spouse's death. This is equivalent to a 10 per cent reduction per year. Thus, a 40-year old survivor could receive a CPP survivor's benefit which is only one-half of the amount which would have been paid if she or he had been age 45 on the contributor's death.
When we look at these provisions today, these benefit calculations and complex eligibility criteria for survivor's benefits may indeed seem discriminatory. They are certainly complex and not easily understood unless you are in the business. However, I believe it is important to keep in mind that the current CPP survivor's benefit provisions were designed in the early 1960, when the flag was designed. Thus, they reflect the social values of that time. Perhaps my hon. friend is right when he says that now is the time to re-examine these proposals because social values have changed.
In any event, in 1960, it was assumed that the surviving spouse of a CPP contributor would be a woman. That is not necessarily true today. It was assumed that that woman prior to the contributor's death had been financially dependent on
her husband's earnings. That is becoming less common today. Thus, legislators decided that the older the spouse the greater the likelihood she could not become financially independent. I think that reasoning is as good today as it was then. Those who were disabled or who had dependent children were also not expected to have the ability to become financially self-sufficient. As a result, these women were provided with the greatest amount of protection under the survivor's benefits provisions. I do not really see anything wrong with that provision, if one is thinking in terms of the cost to the worker of these pensions. Those areas which are most likely to need help should be targeted, which is what the provisions of the CPP did in 1960.
On the other hand, widows under the age of 45 who had no children and who were not disabled were expected to become at least partially responsible for their own financial well-being; and those aged 35 and younger were expected to have the ability to become completely self-sufficient. I am not sure whether that is not an assessment which is even more valid today because there is no doubt about it that today women are better educated, they are out in the workforce and they have better skills. At the age of 35 they are definitely still very employable.
Some of these assumptions may have been perfectly reasonable when the plan was implemented. However, I agree that they may not completely reflect today's values. Today, when a high percentage of women are participating in the paid labour force, the need for lifetime survivor's benefits based strictly on age and/or presence of a disability or dependent children is not really as clear as it was in those days. I do not believe we should look only at the criterion of a surviving spouse being aged 35 to be eligible for CPP protection. We must look at the whole package of survivor's benefits to see how best they can be modified to meet the needs of today's surviving spouse.
As I am sure Hon. Members can appreciate, this is not an easy task. Nevertheless, the Bill before us today asks us to decide whether the current CPP survivor's benefits provisions are out of date and whether or not they should be changed. Because of the complexity of these questions, I am sure Hon. Members realize that the issue of CPP survivor's benefits requires much more study. I can assure Hon. Members that the task force on pensions which reported to the House a year or two ago examined in detail all of the issues flowing from the Canada Pension Plan, including the one brought forward by the Hon. Member. At that time we concluded that the features of the plan with respect to this particular system need not be changed.
For instance, even if a decision is made to change the current system, alternate survivor's benefit provisions must be designed. Like the legislators who put the current plan into effect, we have to determine the needs of CPP contributors and their families and what survivor's benefit protection will best meet those needs.
Of course, as with all major CPP amendments, any future changes to the survivor's benefit provisions must be approved by both the federal Government and two-thirds of the provinces having two-thirds of the population of Canada. Ontario
October 3, 1985

alone can stop any change with respect to the legislation. Hon. Members will recall that the Province did this with respect to another issue.
The Canada Pension Plan belongs to members of the labour force and their families. We must ensure that the plan remains responsive to those people. In any event, I commend the Hon. Member again for bringing this matter before us.
The Canada Pension Plan as devised in 1966 was devised on the basis of what the conditions were at that time. It was well known that in 20 years from that time there would have to be a reassessment. The Hon. Member implied to the House that the Canada Pension Plan was funded, that money was paid in by the workers and their employers and then lent out to the provinces. I can assure the Hon. Member that the Canada Pension Plan is not fully funded. It is far from being fully funded. At the present rate of funding, it would run out of money. In fact, I believe this is the first year the pension plan will pay out more money than it takes in, which is not to say that it is broke or bankrupt. It is merely to say that that is what was planned and that is what is now being reviewed since every so often the plan has to be refinanced.
The Hon. Member opposite also indicated that the interest rate which the provinces pay is very low. Again, I think that is an exaggeration which should be examined. I believe at the moment there is $25 billion in the fund over and above what has been paid out. The provinces have borrowed that money and given back so-called government promissory notes, if you like. They will begin to pay the interest on that money this year, or perhaps they have been paying the interest already. However, they are borrowing that back as well. The interest rates which are paid are adjusted each month to match the rate at which the Government of Canada borrows money on the 25-year bond rate. I admit that is not the market rate and there are higher rates that can be obtained. However, this is a large sum of money about which we are speaking and it is too much to expect to receive the highest rate of interest on that amount in view of the type of risk in which people are interested.
The problem that I see with the CPP is not the amount of interest which it brings in. One of the problems is that it is not fully funded. Right now, it is the best bargain in the world. We now pay only 3.6 per cent-1.8 per cent is paid by the employer and 1.8 per cent is paid by the employee. If the plan were fully funded and if a contributor had to pay for the benefits which he would eventually receive upon retirement, then he would be paying between 9 per cent and 10 per cent of his income. I wonder how many members of the labour force would want to increase their payments to the CPP to 10 per cent. I wonder how many would say: "The plan is getting too rich." That is really what I am saying. If we want to change the plan, then let us look very carefully at what it will cost us and what it will cost the person working in the field. There is no free lunch in this field. At the moment we are depending greatly on an inter-generational gift, as it were. We are hoping that our children will pay sufficient amounts into the fund to provide for us when we retire, just as we have done for past
Canada Pension Plan
generations. When considering this question, we must keep in mind that there are now six people working for every one who is not working, who is retired or who is of preschool age. In the year 2020, when the current workers move out of the workforce and start to look for payments under the Canada Pension Plan, we find that there will probably be only two workers for every person who is retired or is going to school. The question I believe we, as legislators, must ask ourselves is whether those two persons in the workforce would be prepared to pay the kind of money required to provide for all those persons who are not working. I believe that is why we saw in our last Budget a great emphasis on personal savings. That is why we announced plans to revise the RRSPs and other plans to improve private pensions, to provide for portability for two years so that Canadians can move from job to job. This Governemnt realizes the Canada Pension Plan will not be sufficient to really provide what will be expected by those people who retire in the coming years.
We are saying to Canadians that we will look after the Canada Pension Plan. We will continue to improve it but we are asking Canadians to look after their own pensions as well, which we are making possible through tax incentives. It is easy to say we can improve the Canada Pension Plan without looking at the cost. During the tour of our task force we heard from groups who suggested that we double the benefits of the Canada Pension Plan. They said they were prepared to pay 7 per cent, but it would not be 7 per cent. The real cost would be 20 per cent. We can examine the Canada Pension Plan and try to make improvements but let us not do it lightly and carelessly and let us not do it without a real concern for the ultimate cost to the worker and to the employer.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like first to thank my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), for his interest in improving surviving spouse's benefits under the Canada Pension Plan, and for introducing Bill C-247 to supress the age factor impact on those benefits.
My honourable colleague's proposal is no doubt well-intended and most progressive. However, it must be recognized that such a proposal concerns an important component of a very complex system of Government and private programs aimed at protecting widows and widowers.
This systems includes provincial assistance programs, the Federal Old Age Security program, the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan, private pension plans, life insurance policies, and so on. Needless to say, before changing any of those components there should be a very serious study the implications thereof.
I consider it important, Mr. Speaker, to mention that this Government has already changed one of the components in that system. In fact, it has introduced and passed some time

October 3, 1985
Canada Pension Plan
ago Bill C-26, which amends the Old Age Security program to provide for benefit payments to widows and widowers aged 60 to 64 who have little or no income. Many studies had shown that that group of Canadian men and women were among the most in need.
Further, as announced in the Budget speech, the Government will introduce measures to improve minimum standards for private pension funds coming under the federal Pension Benefits Standards Act. Those measures will be of special benefit to the spouses of contributors to those plans.
Concerning such changes, let me refer specifically to the extension of benefits to the surviving spouse before or after the contributor's retirement; to maintaining the benefits in case of remarriage, and to the possibility of sharing pension credits between spouses in cases of regular or common-law marriage breakdown. Those proposals are the result of an extensive consultation process with employers, employees and the general public, undertaken by the Parliamentary Taskforce on Pension Reform. The Government is indeed proving its commitment to improve the income security system for widows and widowers.
I should at this point, Mr. Speaker, look at the surviving spouses' benefits under the Canada Pension Plan, and the importance of the age factor in their determination. Under the current system, once a spouse's qualifications for that benefit have been established, the amount to which the latter will be entitled is figured out on the basis of his or her age.
First, the survivor's pension payable to surviving spouses aged under 65 is determined on the direct basis of the spouse's age at the time the contributor deceased.
This means a surviving spouse aged 45 to 65 will get full benefits made up of two parts: a flat rate component, and a second one based on the deceased contributor's earnings. In 1985, the maximum benefit paid to those surviving spouses totals $250.84 per month.
On the other hand, a surviving spouse aged 35 to 45, having no disability or no dependent child, will have his or her pension reduced by 1/120 for each month short of his or her 45th birthday. A surviving spouse aged 35 or less will not qualify for the survivor's pension before reaching 65, unless he or she is disabled in the meantime.
Finally, when the surviving spouse reaches 65 and qualifies for the Old Age Security basic pension, the surviving spouse's benefit will be re-determined to equal 60 percent of the pension that was or would have been paid to the deceased contributor. The maximum monthly amount of that benefit is $261.25 in the current year.
It is only when we look, as we have just been doing, at the role of the age factor in determining what benefits the surviving spouse will receive that we can appreciate the significance of the reform proposed by the illustrious Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez).
The structure of this provision of the Canada Pension Plan can only be explained by the social climate which existed 20 years ago when the plan was created. Hon. Members will recall that, at the time, few women had a paying job outside the home. They lived in virtually absolute economic dependency and the death of the head of the family left them in a precarious economic position.
As women generally live longer than men and are younger than their husbands, the surviving spouses were at the time mostly women, and in fact, the situation is the same today.
In accordance with these social standards, the contributor had to support his dependents during his years of work. The survivor's pension was therefore considered an extension of this role of provider. Thus, a survivor's pension, a death benefit and an orphan's benefit were incorporated into the system.
However, the originators of the plan deemed it appropriate to limit this responsibility of the contributor to his family. Based on certain premises, an attempt was therefore made to develop an adequate measurement of the state of dependency or the need of the dependents of a contributor.
Based on the fact that it is more difficult to enter the labour market at a later age, it was determined that the older a spouse was, the more dependent she was on the provider.
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry, but I constantly hear a voice to my left and this disturbs my concentration a great deal.
As I was saying, since the possibilities of remarriage decrease with age, it was also determined that, the older the spouse was, the more her chances of finding another provider decreased. This is why the age factor is so important in setting the amount of the survivor's benefits. The older the survivor, the higher the benefits.
Added to the difficulty of entering the labour market because of age, the fact of having dependent children or of being an invalid means economic dependency as these two factors can also affect the possibility of finding a job.
The full pension of a surviving spouse is therefore paid to widows in this situation.
It should also be pointed out, Mr. Speaker, that in the early days of the Plan, the survivor's pension was paid to all widows, but only to invalid widowers. There were therefore two sets of eligibility requirements for this benefit: on one hand, a set for women based on age, the presence of dependent children and invalidity, and on the other hand, a set for men based essentially on invalidity, which, as we have seen, reflected the social standards of the time.
Obviously, society has changed since the 60s, and so has the Canada Pension Plan. In fact, in 1974, the Government amended the Plan to allow a survivor's pension to be paid without regard for the sex of the recipient. There is now only one set of eligibility requirements, namely that which used to apply only to women.
October 3, 1985

I suggest that the original purpose of the survivor's pension, which was to protect the family of a contributor against financial hardship resulting from his or her death, is still valid today. However, because of the increased presence of women in the labour force and the new economic weight of the wife both in the family and society, we must reconsider the validity of the age factor in computing the pension the surviving spouse should get. It should be emphasized, however, that the scales now in use are still adequate for a category of surviving spouses, that of generally older widows who have never been part of the labour force.
At first glance, the proposal put forward by my hon. friend would seem to correct an injustice. Its adoption, however, would raise several questions concerning the purpose of this pension which, as I said, is to protect the family of the contributor against any economic hardship resulting from his or her death. Because the age factor is there to determine the level of dependency or need, Mr. Speaker, I doubt very much that we could abolish this factor without updating the basic assumptions and the structure of the benefits to the surviving spouse to reflect today's economic and social reality.
I should mention at this point that even though the Federal Government may propose changes to the Canada Pension Plan, such changes could only come into force with the consent of two-thirds of the provinces that have two-thirds of the population of the country. Discussions between the two levels of Government are therefore necessary, particularly in view of the fact that in would be preferable to maintain a sort of parity between the Canadian Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan. Such changes would therefore require a more in depth study of the benefits structure by the two levels of government.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that we should act with utmost care, because this scheme and the Quebec Pension Plan affect the workers of the whole country. I am also convinced that, in co-operation with the provinces, we can meet the current needs of the surviving spouses and thus carry out successfully a major component of the pension reform.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will just say a few words because I would like to have this Bill voted upon in the House. The Speaker who was in the chair prior to you said that there was some doubt concerning the motion because it may involve a government prerogative. He meant that this entails an expenditure of government funds. If that is considered to be a Government prerogative, I am afraid that 99 per cent of the motions brought before the House would have to be disallowed. Practically every Bill introduced, if enacted, would involve an expenditure of Government funds.
The Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) who introduced this Bill asked what is so magical about the age 35. I think we have got off track today. This Bill is about disability benefits. I am sure the hon. gentleman will agree that the
Canada Pension Plan
section which he cited is about disability benefits. The Hon. Member is asking what is so magical about the age 35. If you are two or three days less than 35 you are treated differently than if you are 35.
I would like to add to what the hon. gentleman said and perhaps supply him with some more ammunition for this particular argument before the House today. The section which he wants to amend says:
-if the surviving spouse
(i)	has reached 65 years of age, or
(ii)	in the case of a surviving spouse who has not reached 65 years of age,
(A)	had at the time of the death of the contributor reached 35 years of age.
(B)	was at the time of the death of the contributor a surviving spouse with dependent children, or
(C)	is disabled;
The "or" does not come between (A) and (B). It says "or (C) is disabled". You must meet the above two conditions and then it says "or (C) is disabled". The question, Mr. Speaker, is what is so magical about the age of 35.
My point is that the hon. gentleman said that this will not involve an expenditure of Government funds because, as he so correctly pointed out, the Canada Pension Plan now has an overabundance of money in it, as it always has. What have they done with the money? There were new agreements signed recently to allow the provincial governments to borrow cheap money from that fund which is contibuted to by the workers of Canada.
Let us narrow it down to only the disability pension. I will alert the hon. gentleman to a fact that I am sure he is aware of, but which he can perhaps use in future arguments. We are talking about disability benefits. A person fighting for a disability pension has to go through quite a procedure before he establishes his entitlement. He must get letters from this doctor and that doctor and then an independent doctor and then another doctor and then another doctor. It is appealed and eventually the person, who may have been on his back in bed for many years and cannot move at all, gets his disability pension.
However, that person may have had to get social assistance to support his family, as most such people do. When it is determined that he was qualified for disability pension from the time that the applied, which may have been two or three years ago, the department sends his cheque to the provincial government to repay what he received while he was on his back having to draw that little amount of social assistance and welfare.

speechtext: Shameful.

In this new spirit of co-operation between the federal and provincial Governments it is easy. You do not even have to sign a form now. There is an agreement between the federal Government and the provincial Governments. All you need do is find out that he drew social assistance.

October 3, 1985
Canada Pension Plan
Some of the financial wizards in this Chamber should be asking another basic question about that. The federal Government pays 50 per cent of social assistance. We now get to the point. Half of the money that fellow on his back in bed received came from the federal treasury under the Canada Assistance Plan as every Member knows.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: They got it twice.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is catching on. Now, along comes this disability pension which the man has been trying to get all along. What happens? The entire amount he gets is then transferred from the federal to the provincial treasury.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: So what is your point?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is pretty slow. What you are doing is paying 50 per cent of what he got and then 100 per cent. What is more disgusting is that you look for a way that the money can be recovered and you cannot find one. It is a transfer from the Department of National Health and Welfare to the provincial Department of Finance.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: What has this got to do with the Bill?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Very simply this. The Government of Canada cannot see that to do this would not cost any more than what it is already transferring directly from the CPP to the coffers of the provincial Department of Social Services. In other words, the whole thing would not cost the federal treasury anything at all. What is obvious here, however, is that someone involved in this new spirit of co-operation should explain how a disabled person can draw social assistance with the federal treasury paying 50 per cent, and then all of a sudden the federal treasury is reimbursing the provincial government for 150 per cent. It is an interesting question.
There is absolutely nothing wrong with this Bill. Absolutely nothing at all. I think that we should vote on it and the Speaker will have to rule if this is a government prerogative or not, but it removes from the CPP a grave inequity based on age. It is not going to cost the Government of Canada anything at all if we pass this hon. gentleman's Bill and I congratulate him for bringing it to the Chamber.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a distinct pleasure to follow in debate such speakers as the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) and the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker), not to mention the excellent speakers from the Okanagan and Quebec. One cannot help reflecting on the fact that the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt has brought an important issue before us. I think all Members agree that the age related provision referred to may have had some wisdom 20 years ago, but that has clearly changed in 1985. It also struck me, speaking immediately after the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate, that the provision was put in place 20 years ago by a Liberal Government. They had 20 years to correct it, but all of a sudden, early in the month of October, 1985, a Member discovers the legislation
was flawed from the beginning. It is still flawed today and he was part of the caucus which did nothing about it for such a long time.
I urge Members of this Chamber to take the concern raised by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt seriously, but at the same time I urge them not to pass this legislation. How can I have those two thoughts simultaneously? It is because I have thought about the concept of the stewardship which Members of Parliament have over public funds. The first question I ask myself is: Who are the owners of this fund? Do the Canadian taxpayers own the CPP fund? My conclusion is that they do not. Some Canadians, part of the workforce, contribute to this fund and, in the final analysis, they are in reality the owners of the fund.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: So Canadians own it.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Is the stewardship of this fund in the hands of Members of the Parliament of Canada?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: You lost me, brother.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA PENSION PLAN MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I suggest it is not. The people who designed this fund some 20 years ago decided that the stewardship was to be in the hands of a combination of elected members from both provincial and federal legislatures. I lived through a period in this Chamber of some four and a half years under increasing distress over the trend in Canada to act unilaterally, to ignore the stewardship of the provinces, whether it was constitutional, agreed to, or whatever. I saw my country begin to fall apart economically, emotionally and in every other way, partly as a consequence of a House of Commons dominated by one Party dedicated to the principle of unilateral action rather than respect for provincial jurisdiction. If this Bill were the best idea in the world and completely unflawed-and I suggest it is flawed-it would still be wrong for members of this Chamber to act unilaterally to change these arrangements. Until there is an agreement between the federal and provincial Governments then we should be reluctant to act. The Government which was elected a year ago declared during the election campaign that it would act in a manner designed to restore respect between the two levels of Government, respect for jurisdiction and respect for agreements entered into. It has done that and done it well. Because that climate of confidence and co-operation has been restored there is every reason to believe that we will come to a collective decision on changes to the fund in a coherent and systematic way, changes for the better in the future. Until you have that kind of discussion, until you work in that way, there is always the danger of going off on a flight of fancy in the belief that you are doing good when in reality you are doing harm.
This particular proposal simply to drop the requirements for benefits puts financial strain on the fund. One of its consequences could be a reduction in the contribution to anyone who is entitled to it.
