subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF CONTRACT AWARDS. (B) CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
THE ADMINISTRATION-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF CONTRACT AWARDS. (B) CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the adjournment debate tonight. My question relates to a most unsatisfactory reply given by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) on September 16, as reported at page 6644 of Hansard. At that time I asked why it was that the new conflict of interest guidelines for Cabinet Ministers were deficient. I brought two matters to his attention.
The new conflict of interest guidelines, which I have in my possession, are designed in such a way as to ensure that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and Cabinet Ministers do not appoint their relatives to cushy jobs, as they have been doing in the most abominable way since last year. In their first six months in office the Tories have appointed no less than 1,200 hacks, flacks, bagmen and relatives to various jobs. They are all listed in the Black Paper on Tory patronage. Some of those 1,200 people were relatives of Cabinet Ministers. In the new conflict of fnterest guidelines, the Prime Minister indicated that in the future it would not be permissible for a Minister to hire his relatives or the relatives of his Cabinet colleagues. The biggest deficiency in the program is what happens to the relatives of Cabinet Ministers who have already been hired.
As we know, the brother of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has been appointed to a very lucrative position to do legal work for and on behalf of the Government of Canada or an agency of the Government, namely, the 1988 Olympics. This has happened in other areas as well.
It will not be possible in the future to appoint people such as those who were hired in the past. In other words, the Prime Minister said that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) is wrong in trying to appoint his sons, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is wrong in practising this nepotism and that it could not happen in the future. If it is wrong in the future, why are those people permitted to keep their jobs now? I am sure you agree, Mr. Speaker, that they should not keep
Adjournment Debate
their jobs and that this is a terrible loophole in the conflict of interest guidelines.
There is another loophole as well, and it is an even more important one. I am referring to the entire means of reviewing political appointments. In his reply on September 16, the Deputy Prime Minister said:
-that the entire range of all appointments which have been made are going to be subject to a review by the parliamentary process to see how it works.
This is not the case. Only certain people who have been appointed will be reviewed by the parliamentary process, that is, those appointed by Order in Council. Those people on contracts are not reviewable. As a matter of fact, a large number of people on contract did not even tender for their jobs.
We heard of an instance lately where officials in the Prime Minister's Office are not on salary but are on contract. Therefore, people on contract do not have to adhere to the conflict of interest guidelines. That situation is not even covered in the new conflict of interest book. Of course this means that if a Cabinet Minister wants to hire someone and wants the person not to be subjected to the provisions of the conflict of interest guidelines, all the Minister has to do is say to his or her friend: "Get yourself a contracting business and then I will hire your business on contract". Of course the business may have only one person working in it. In that event, the conflict of interest guidelines are totally bypassed, thereby defeating what the Prime Minister said in the House. I take it, Mr. Speaker, that he was indicating that in good faith. He said in this House that he was going to end this kind of thing. He has not.
We need revisions to those guidelines to make sure that they work because there are these two gigantic loopholes which I have just described and about which the Deputy Prime Minister made a completely erroneous reply. He had it all backwards. He had assumed that everyone who was appointed would be up for review. I am sure that the Parliamentary Secretary sitting across from me would recognize that that is a mistake the Deputy Prime Minister made, so I will now give him the opportunity to correct the record and to state the truth. Hopefully he will state that the Prime Minister will review these conflict of interest guidelines to ensure that they work and put an end in the future to the nepotism practised in the past and the present and to ensure that people cannot bypass the guidelines by simply getting themselves hired by contract.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF CONTRACT AWARDS. (B) CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset that this newfound interest of the Liberal Party in tight guidelines is very amusing to those of us who were here over the past five years.
The question which my hon. friend raised confuses several matters and I want to make four points.

October 3, 1985
Adjournment Debate
The Government, until the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) brought in his measures, has been operating under the regime established by its predecessor.

subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF CONTRACT AWARDS. (B) CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
speechtext: And even it was broken.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF CONTRACT AWARDS. (B) CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
speechtext:
I find that it is interesting that my friends who find themselves in opposition now have come to embrace as a virtue what they never practised in fact. None of the suggestions which they have advanced were adopted by the Liberal Party in the decades during which they were in office. I appreciate that had the Hon. Member been a member of the Liberal Party federally he would have made sure that those guidelines were tightened under the Right Hon. Pierre Trudeau. I can just see the Hon. Member taking Prime Minister Trudeau to task on that; yes, I can just envision that.
The measures placed before the House by Prime Minister Mulroney on September 9 constituted the most comprehensive and far-reaching treatment of public sector ethics ever pronounced in a Canadian Parliament.

subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF CONTRACT AWARDS. (B) CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
speechtext: How can you state that with a straight face?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF CONTRACT AWARDS. (B) CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
speechtext:
After great research, my friend.
The new conflict of interest code makes specific provision to ensure that those working for the Government under contract are bound by the appropriate provisions respecting both conflict of interest and post-employment considerations. I refer to Section 10 of the code.
My friend, Mr. Speaker, suggests that we are closing the barn door after the horses have gone. Under the Liberal Party the barn never had a door, and we have taken steps to refine the appointment process. My colleague refers to it as a loophole. Nonsense. We have brought in a review process which was not there during all the years of the previous Liberal Government.

subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF CONTRACT AWARDS. (B) CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
speechtext: What about the relations?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF CONTRACT AWARDS. (B) CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
speechtext:
Where was the appointments process under the previous Liberal Government? Obviously it was not there. I remind my hon. friend that we are a Government which has come to office with the support of hundreds of thousands of Canadians. We have 211 seats from across the country and naturally we are going to find ourselves with many friends. This is a Party with many friends. We make no apologies for that. Because the Hon. Member across the way finds himself without friends, that is the a difficulty he is going to have, not only for the balance of this Parliament but probably for years to come.
I suggest to him that our process of political accountability and the regime that we have set in place for outreaches anything ever done under the previous Liberal Government. We suggest that there is some room for improvement. We are going to try the process. We will look for improvement. However, under the previous Liberal Government, there was never any suggestion of this kind of accountability.

subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-COMMISSIONER'S REPORT (A) REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION (B) FRENCH AS LANGUAGE OF WORK IN PUBLIC SERVICE

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-COMMISSIONER'S REPORT (A) REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION (B) FRENCH AS LANGUAGE OF WORK IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 27 of this year, nearly six months ago, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) about a very important matter, namely the Report of the Commissioner of Official Languages and the need to amend the legislation in order to broaden the Commissioner's powers.
Mr. Speaker, in the Fifth Report of the Special Joint Committee on Official Languages, recommendations 12 to 18 were aimed precisely at strengthening the role of the Commissioner and giving him more power, thus enabling him to carry out his parliamentary mandate in an effective and efficient manner.
Mr. Speaker, the House will recall that the Prime Minister answered, as reported in Hansard on page 3412, that he considered this a very important issue, extremement impor-tante, to quote him directly, and he reminded me that in the Throne Speech, the Government had announced its intention to take action, and he then informed the House that he had that very morning asked a committee of deputy ministers to examine the entire question of amendments to the legislation, amendments which had, in fact, been proposed by the Committee on Official Languages.
Mr. Speaker, the result was that in May, I believe, the committee was established under the chairmanship of Mrs. Huguette Labelle, who is now Chairman of the Public Service Commission. The committee included several deputy ministers from Treasury Board, the Department of the Secretary of State, the Prime Minister's Office and the Privy Council. The Committee referred to by the Prime Minister was set up, I am told, in April, met from that time until July, with a mandate to examine the recommendations of the Committee on Official Languages and also, probably as part of a broader mandate, to examine relations between the federal Government and official language groups and groups that were basically the responsibility of the Secretary of State.
As far as I know, the committee's meetings were held in camera. To date, none of us know what transpired during those meetings, and this evening, I would like to ask the Parliamentary Secretary the following: Could he give us a report on the proceedings to date, and perhaps on any recommendations made by the committee? Who is the chairman, now that Mrs. Huguette Labelle has left? Is it Mr. Gerard Veilleux? There is a rather important question which should be answered: What have been the results of the committee's work to date, and is there perhaps a possibility that the committee of deputy ministers could appear before the Committee on Official Languages to provide some clarification and
October 3, 1985

release or provide details and perhaps inform Hon. Members of the important work they have done?
I therefore invite the Parliamentary Secretary to answer this question: Is he prepared to give the House the assurance this evening that the Chairman of the Committee, Mr. Gerard Veilleux, or someone else, will appear before the Committee to explain what they have accomplished to date?
In the second part of my question I dealt with another aspect of the report of the Commissioner of Official Languages. It is indeed a very important issue-the language of work in the Public Service of Canada. God knows, Mr. Speaker, that the members of the Committee on Official Languages had been concerned over that matter for a long time. We had asked the Government for clear and specific directives with respect to the Government's political intentions, the real intentions of this Government to assist, encourage and even prod certain departments so that public employees might be able to work in the language of their choice, their mother tongue normally being the one they know best!
In answer to my question the Prime Minister said, and I quote from page 3412:
If people cannot work in French, it is a myth, and everything must be done to maintain the integrity of that instrument, that cultural and linguistic wealth, either by coercion, or by making sure that it will be sought after as an instrument of work.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct another question to the Parliamentary Secretary and ask him whether the Government is through studying the question of language of work, whether it is prepared to share once again with the Committee on Official Languages Policy and Programs its expertise and knowledge, and tell us which way it is headed. Hon. Members are interested in knowing what this Government intends to do about the official languages. We want to know where we stand and what we should do to uphold, promote and expand this right which I consider important to public employees, namely to receive communications from their superiors in their own language, to be able to work in French or in English in their office and thus meet the basic criterion of the Act: Not only must the public be served in English and French in this country, but public employees must also enjoy the right and privilege to be able to work in their mother tongue.
Mr. Speaker, I might point out that 90 per cent of Government working documents are in English. It will take some political will to change the bad habit of thinking that everybody speaks the majority language, which is English.
Let us not forget either how awkward it is for Francophones, and not just unilingual Francophones but also Anglophones who speak French well, when a unilingual Anglophone joins a group of bilingual Anglophones and Francophones who are having a conversation in French in an office situation and all the participants in the conversation adopt the language of the single non bilingual person in the group. This often happens whenever a unilingual Anglophone joins a group of 8, 9 or 10 Francophone civil servants who are having a conversation in French in an office situation; everybody switches to English.
Adjournment Debate
Such an attitude is not conducive to making French a language of work in the Public Service.
In bilingual areas, Mr. Speaker, and this is the last point I should like to make, the use of French at the work place has not increased much since 1978. I should like, therefore, the Parliamentary Secretary to advise us whether the Government intends to amend the legislation to make French a language of work in the Public Service.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-COMMISSIONER'S REPORT (A) REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION (B) FRENCH AS LANGUAGE OF WORK IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to first suggest to my hon. friend that I am not able at this time to bring him up to date with respect to the deliberations of the committee to which he refers. However, I will make inquiries to see what additional information can be sent to him.
As far as his comments are concerned with respect to the language of work, I will also ask that any further information in that regard be brought to his attention.
In reply to the Hon. Member's question, I wish to state that we are proud of the efforts this Government has made with respect to the official languages program. The Speech from the Throne of November 5, 1984, on the first day of the Thirty-third Session of Parliament, placed the issue in the context of national unity. We indicated our commitment as a Government to ensuring that the equality of the two official languages so vital to our national character and our identity is respected in fact as well as in law. At that time, the Government acknowledged the need for ongoing improvements and for vigilance in this crucial area of our national life.
With respect to the question of law, I suggest that the equality of English and French are already recognized by the Constitution of Canada, as well as by the Official Languages Act. As far as the question of implementation is concerned, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) in speaking before the Joint Committee on Official Languages last May made it clear that the Government intends to review all aspects of the official languages program, to reassess the priorities and improve its effectiveness and efficiency.
When it comes to the language of work we are dealing with a longstanding and difficult issue which, as my hon. friend knows as a result of his interest and involvement in the Official Language Committee, is not amenable to simple or quick solutions.
Having said that, I am pleased to inform the House that the Treasury Board is taking measures to improve the language of work situation in the federal Public Service. We published a catalogue of departmental language of work initiatives in March of this year. It was distributed to departments to suggest ways and means of improving the use of both official languages in the workplace.
Furthermore, the secretariat's analysis of the 1985-86 official languages plan provided evidence that senior departmental managers are giving increasing consideration to

October 3, 1985
Adjournment Debate
measures which would improve opportunities for their employees to work in their preferred official language.
Mr. Speaker, I have further notes with respect to this matter which I will be pleased to provide to my hon. colleague.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-(A) CLOSING OF A PLANT IN MONTREAL BY BOMBARDIER (B) PURCHASE OF LOCOMOTIVES FROM BOMBARDIER-GOVERNMENT'S POSITION
TRANSPORT-(A) CLOSING OF A PLANT IN MONTREAL BY BOMBARDIER (B) PURCHASE OF LOCOMOTIVES FROM BOMBARDIER-GOVERNMENT'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier today I asked a question from the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Blais-Grenier), concerning the Bombardier company, which has not received any help from the Government of Canada and which must now close its locomotive manufacturing plant.
The answer given by the Minister of State, the Hon. Member for Rosemont, is utterly disgraceful. My colleague and friend, the Hon. Member for St. Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), shares my views on the subject and this is why I am challenging immediately tonight in this adjournment debate, the answer given by the Minister. She said, and I quote:
The Bombardier decisions in this case were made in accordance with the best industrial development criteria.
In other words, the lay off of some 1,000 employees in the east end of Montreal does not trouble the Minister, because it follows the best criteria from industrial development.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-(A) CLOSING OF A PLANT IN MONTREAL BY BOMBARDIER (B) PURCHASE OF LOCOMOTIVES FROM BOMBARDIER-GOVERNMENT'S POSITION
speechtext: The Schefferville formula.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-(A) CLOSING OF A PLANT IN MONTREAL BY BOMBARDIER (B) PURCHASE OF LOCOMOTIVES FROM BOMBARDIER-GOVERNMENT'S POSITION
speechtext:
Exactly. My colleague, who is in charge of labour questions, is here tonight and shares my view. We are reminded of the attitude held by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he shut down the Schefferville plant after reaping millions for the American company and firing hundreds of workers. This is according to the best criteria for industrial development.
And the Minister of State for Transport has the gall to add;
We had lengthy discussions with Bombardier representatives who pointed out to us that there was no other solution.
Mr. Speaker, certainly there were alternatives because this industry, which has been in operation in Montreal since the turn of this century, has always been a viable and profitable industry providing jobs to thousands of workers in the east end of Montreal. And the previous Government never hesitated to prescribe guidelines to railways such as the CN, the Canadian National Railways, a Crown corporation that can get its guidelines from the Government, or give instructions in particular to VIA Rail which has recently bought locomotives from General Motors instead of Bombardier.
If those two Crown corporations, VIA Rail and CN, which further have their headquarters in Montreal, had received
instructions from the Minister of State for Transport or the Prime Minister of Canada, the company would not be about to shut down its plant. Hundreds of workers who have been working for years in that plant would not now be forced to look for other jobs.
The steelworkers' union, under the good guidance of their director, Mr. Clement Godbout, has issued a very outspoken press release. It stated: We have had here in the Bombardier plant two and three successive generations of workers who have acquired an outstanding expertise in the area of freight locomotives. We have a manpower that is qualified, available and responsible. Bombardier's proposal to shut down the plant must be stifled." And the steelworkers' union is asking the Government to meet its responsibilities and help them save their plant. This is exactly what I was asking the Minister of State for Transport today, since she has the means and the time to travel to Europe at the expense of Canadian taxpayers.
If the Minister had taken it upon herself this summer to go to Paris or Stockholm to sell Bombardier locomotives, I would have been the first to congratulate her today. However, the Minister strutted about in Europe at the expense of the Crown and the Canadian taxpayers and did not bother about the workers of her own constituency and the ridings of Eastern Montreal, who are now unemployed because the Progressive Conservative Government has abandoned the Bombardier Company.
Jean-Guy Dubuc, editorial writer of La Presse, spoke about this issue in an article titled:
If only Bombardier been helped ... Bombardier will stop making freight locomotives.
Which means hundreds of jobs lost and hundreds more unemployed in Eastern Montreal.
As though Canada, the country with the second longest railways in the world, could afford to lose such a technology and such an industry.
Indeed, the question is: Does the Government-
-the Conservative Government, that is-
-have the right to close down a major industrial sector by refusing to support a company faced with American competition?
The answer is obvious, Mr. Speaker. The Conservative Government has no right to abandon Bombardier, it has no right to put out of work some 1,000 workers who have been earning an honest living by manufacturing locomotives, and I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to tell us that this Government will accept its responsibilities and instruct VIA Rail and the Canadian National to purchase good locomotives made in Montreal by good specialized workers.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: TRANSPORT-(A) CLOSING OF A PLANT IN MONTREAL BY BOMBARDIER (B) PURCHASE OF LOCOMOTIVES FROM BOMBARDIER-GOVERNMENT'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that there were not more people in the House to hear a vintage speech by my

October 3, 1985

colleague who is a much better speaker in Opposition than he was as a Minister. However, I am surprised that he is playing politics with this very serious matter. I know that I speak for all Members of the House when I state that we share the concern that has been raised by my colleague for those workers at Bombardier who have been displaced by the company's decision-and I emphasize that it was the company's decision-not to continue its operations in the heavy locomotive field and to focus its attention on other markets. I will discuss the assistance that is coming to those other markets in a minute.
It is worth noting that the problems encountered by Bombardier in supplying a technologically efficient diesel locomotive did not occur overnight. This is a field in which technology is always advancing. As a matter of form, I would like to ask the Member what the Liberal Government did during the past 17 years to assist Bombardier in acquiring or developing the technological expertise to compete in Canadian and international diesel locomotive markets. I am not speaking only of directives but of technological improvements, because directives come easy to some political parties. It is technological improvements that will help this country to proceed.
I point out to my hon. colleague, Mr. Speaker, that Bombardier was consulted on the possibility of participating in VIA
Adjournment Debate
Rail's recent order for new locomotives. I am advised as well that in 1984 Canadian National offered Bombardier the opportunity to build 15 new locomotives. CN was going to work with Bombardier in developing an acceptable design. Once again in 1985 CN asked Bombardier to quote on the design and construction of 20 locomotives. The Government cannot force a company to quote on business.
The decision to close the Bombardier locomotive plant reflected the company's decision not to compete with the other domestic locomotive companies. It did not in any way represent an abandonment by the Government of any of our commitments to this industry.
Finally, I would point out to my colleagues that VIA Rail's pending order for new rail passenger rolling stock will be procured exclusively from a consortium made up of Bombardier and UTDC companies. There is no question that the Government is continuing its commitment to give the workers of Bombardier every opportunity to keep their jobs.
